Release and change control
IDs are permanent and are not recycled. Material changes require a versioned change record, source authority, backward-compatibility decision, and regenerated trace/validation artifacts. Appendix S remains the authoritative research and calibration queue; an open issue does not silently acquire a default value.
Executive Abstract
The National Health Assurance Framework specifies a proposed public U.S. healthcare system centered on continuous public default coverage and zero or near-zero point-of-care cost for covered medically necessary care. It combines national financing and standards with regional administration, state/regional/tribal transition compacts, a four-unit diagnostic-treatment network, a specialist-routing backplane, hospital global budgets and public-service charters, national purchasing and public medicines capacity, expanded benefits, and a federated information mesh.
The architecture separates operations, disbursement, oversight, scorekeeping, innovation, transition command, congressional accountability, and adjudication. It treats transition protection, legitimacy and safety, and adaptation and repair as system layers with enforceable controls rather than as post-implementation add-ons. AI may assist clinical and administrative work, but accountable humans and public institutions retain authority, explanation, review, and remedy duties.
The controlled cost position is a framework modeling assumption: approximately $4.75 trillion per year at mature steady state in real 2024 dollars, with a plausible range of $4.30–$5.25 trillion; $1.2–$2.0 trillion of transition and implementation cost over 10–12 years; and a first-decade transition-adjusted annual range of approximately $4.90–$5.05 trillion. The simulation specification is designed to test these assumptions, not to hard-code them as achieved results.
The release is both a public-facing policy explanation, a systems-engineering specification, and a machine-usable reference. It defines assumptions, stakeholder needs, project/system/verification requirements, performance and cost parameters, architecture elements, interfaces, phases, risks, scenarios, data rights, comparator rules, state variables, outputs, schemas, uncertainty conventions, the named 200-family PMC manufacturing portfolio, and public-dashboard controls. Bidirectional traceability and executable validation code accompany the document so another software or AI agent can reproduce the release and implement a comparative simulation.
Framework at a Glance
PLAIN-LANGUAGE ORIENTATION  The framework is a proposed public health-assurance system, not a single agency that owns every hospital or makes every clinical decision. It separates the body that operates coverage, the office that pays, the institutions that protect rights and review performance, the authority that manages transition, the agency that funds innovation, and the court that can issue enforceable remedies.
For a patient, the intended experience is straightforward: coverage exists by default; covered medically necessary care normally has no point-of-care price; a nearby diagnostic-treatment unit or ordinary provider supplies the front door; a structured specialist route is used when additional expertise is needed; and a denial, delay, privacy violation, or payment failure carries an explanation and an appeal path.
The institutional structure is deliberately less simple than a single national health agency because concentrating operations, payment, performance certification, rights enforcement, fiscal reserve control, and judicial remedy in one chain of command would recreate conflicts that the framework is designed to remove.
Table FM-4. The nine top-level institutions in one page

| Institution | Public question | Primary answer |

| DNHA | Who runs coverage and national operating programs? | Enrollment, coverage, claims rules, care-delivery policy, medicines, workforce, records, and regional operations. |

| NHAC | Who protects people from the operating system? | Independent rights, privacy, safety, anti-fraud, ombudsman, provisional relief, and public reporting. |

| NBIA | Who funds innovation without embedding monopoly price in every medicine? | Public R&D, trials, comparative evidence, secure research, and public-interest licensing. |

| THDO | Who sends the money? | A mandatory Treasury payment rail for authorized provider, hospital, pharmacy, and other obligations. |

| NHETF | What absorbs fiscal and operational shocks? | Operating stabilization, transition/shock reserves, and the long-run health endowment. |

| NHTCA | Who protects the changeover? | Patient, provider, hospital, pharmacy, worker, employer, data, state, regional, and tribal continuity. |

| NHASB | Who measures and repairs the framework? | Independent scorekeeping, formula control, reviews, red teams, sunsets, and bounded repair. |

| CHAO | Who watches executive compliance for Congress? | Legislative-branch monitoring of interference, impoundment, vacancies, reporting, and statutory performance. |

| Article I Court | Where can an enforceable remedy be obtained? | Expedited patient, provider, payment, entitlement, and anti-impoundment adjudication. |
Figure FM-1. Nine-institution operating and accountability context

Table FM-5. Three ordinary system journeys

| Journey | Sequence | Why the separation matters |

| Care | Automatic/provisional coverage → provider or unit → specialist/hospital when needed → longitudinal record | Coverage authority cannot create appointments by itself, so capacity and routing are explicit operating systems. |

| Payment | Authorized service or budget → obligation record → THDO disbursement → provider/pharmacy/hospital | The entity deciding a claim does not control whether Treasury honors the resulting lawful payment. |

| Challenge | Notice and explanation → ombudsman/provisional relief → administrative review when retained → Article I remedy | Operations cannot be the final judge of their own denial, delay, privacy, or payment conduct. |

How to use this document
The specification is intentionally redundant at the metadata level but not at the narrative level. Core concepts are explained once in the body, then referenced by stable IDs in registers, matrices, appendices, and simulation records. Readers should use the body for meaning and the appendices for controlled lookup and machine transfer.
Table D1-4. Audience-specific reading paths

| Audience | Primary sections | Primary use |

| Policy and legislative readers | Executive Abstract; Sections 1–3, 6, 8, 9, 12, 13 | Understand purpose, design choices, financing, legal structure, conclusions, and implications. |

| Systems engineers and architects | Front Matter; Section 4; Sections 7, 10, 11; Appendices B–K and P–Q | Evaluate entities, functions, interfaces, requirements, allocation, verification, risk, and model structure. |

| Clinicians and care operators | Sections 2, 4.6, 6.1–6.11, 7, 10 | Evaluate patient pathways, workload, safety, escalation, specialist access, hospital operations, and transition. |

| Economists and fiscal analysts | Sections 3, 5, 8, 11; Appendices F–H and Q | Evaluate assumptions, parameterization, financing, reserves, offsets, uncertainty, and comparative outputs. |

| Legal analysts | Sections 4.9–4.10, 9, 10; Appendices L and O | Evaluate authority, preemption, rights, remedies, anti-impoundment, continuity, contingencies, and repair. |

| Simulation builders | Traceability and Simulation Conventions; Sections 5, 8, 11; Appendices B–J, P–Q | Translate objects, variables, parameters, scenarios, equations, and evidence into executable models. |

| Verification and oversight bodies | Sections 4.10, 5.3–5.6, 7.3–7.4, 10; Appendices D–J, P, R | Verify requirements, phase gates, risk controls, public measures, and corrective actions. |

| Patients, advocates, and public readers | Executive Abstract; Sections 1, 2, 6.1–6.11, 12, 13; Appendix R | Understand rights, access pathways, accountability, impacts, tradeoffs, and public reporting. |
Standard anatomy of substantive sections
Every substantive section will use the following sequence unless a section's purpose makes a field inapplicable. Inapplicable fields will be stated rather than silently omitted.
Purpose of the section and decision question.
Human-readable explanation of the framework concept or problem.
System entities and interfaces involved.
Applicable ASM assumptions and source classification.
Data, variables, units, model parameters, targets, and external evidence.
PR/SR/VR and KPP/TPP linkages.
Principal risks, failure modes, mitigations, and open issues.
Simulation implications, including comparator treatment and sensitivity needs.
Normative language
Table D1-5. Normative and interpretive terms

| Term | Meaning in this specification |

| Shall | Mandatory requirement. A shall-statement must be uniquely identified, verifiable, allocated, and traceable. |

| Should | Recommended design or practice that is not yet a mandatory requirement. Deviations require rationale when material. |

| May | Permitted option within stated limits; it does not establish an obligation. |

| Will | Forecast, expected sequence, or statement of intent; not a substitute for a requirement. |

| Target | Desired or required performance value at a defined time and scope; not an observed baseline or forecast. |

| Assumption | A design or modeling premise that remains labeled until verified or revised. |

| To be calibrated | A required parameter or threshold whose numerical value has not been responsibly established. |

| Open issue | A material unresolved decision; later drafting must not invent a definitive answer. |
Reading and interpretation rules
The source hierarchy governs conflicts. Later prose may elaborate a controlled object but may not silently contradict its register entry.
A quantitative statement must be read together with its classification, unit, price year, population, geography, time, and uncertainty treatment.
Zero or near-zero point-of-care cost does not mean zero resource cost or unlimited instantaneous capacity.
A requirement target is not a promise that simulation results will achieve the target. The simulation tests whether the architecture can plausibly do so under stated inputs.
Omission from a summary does not delete a controlled object. Registers and appendices are authoritative for object existence and status.
External evidence supports empirical claims; it does not become framework design authority unless a controlled change adopts it.

Definitions
DEFINITION RULE  Definitions control the use of terms throughout later deliverables. A substantive section may add operational detail, equations, or legal language, but it must not change a defined concept without a recorded revision.
Table D1-7. Controlled framework definitions

| Term | Controlled definition |

| Adaptation and repair | Layer 5 governance functions that measure performance, maintain formulas, review rules and technologies, test contingencies, close corrective actions, and modify the system through legally bounded change control. |

| Adaptation waiver | A time-limited regional deviation from a national implementation method that preserves national rights and performance floors, states a testable hypothesis, defines endpoints and safeguards, and receives independent evaluation. |

| Administrative private-plan role | A certified fixed-fee or delegated service role performed for the public system without transferring the public entitlement or permitting the contractor to determine high-stakes rights outside public rules and review. |

| Architecture element | A uniquely identified institution, office, authority, fund, court, operational network, service, or infrastructure component assigned responsibilities within the framework. |

| Assumption | A proposition accepted for framework design or simulation until verified, revised, or rejected. Assumptions are not presented as external facts unless evidence independently supports them. |

| Baseline | The defined measurement of the existing U.S. healthcare system against which framework outcomes are compared, including the reference year, population, geography, service scope, price basis, and data source. |

| Benefit boundary | The rule-defined line between covered medically necessary care, conditionally covered care, supplemental services, and excluded services, together with the evidence, explanation, and appeal process used to place services on either side. |

| Capacity ledger | A regionally maintained, auditable representation of available specialist, facility, diagnostic, transport, and other constrained service capacity by time, location, service class, and urgency allocation. |

| Clinically linked social support | A nonclinical support financed by the framework only when documented medical need, care-plan linkage, time boundary, expected health effect, and accountable owner distinguish it from general social policy. |

| Comparator system | The existing U.S. healthcare system model used for side-by-side simulation under aligned population, time, economic, service, and outcome assumptions. |

| Continuous coverage | Core public coverage that persists without loss due to employment change, income churn, interstate movement, family-status change, disability, pregnancy, aging, or legacy-payer status. |

| Core benefit | The nationally guaranteed set of covered medically necessary services, products, and supports financed and administered under the public entitlement. |

| Cost offset | A reduction in spending in one modeled category attributable to a specified intervention or outcome in another category. Offsets must identify timing, attribution, uncertainty, and whether they are cash, budgetary, or total-system effects. |

| Covered medically necessary care | Care, products, diagnostics, transport, or clinically linked supports that meet the framework's statutory benefit criteria and are subject to transparent coverage, evidence, safety, and appeal rules. |

| Data right | An enforceable patient or public entitlement concerning access, correction, consent, segmentation, use limitation, audit visibility, portability, notice, or remedy for health information. |

| Dedicated revenue sufficiency | The ratio of dedicated framework receipts and authorized transfers to certified obligations for the applicable period. |

| Deemed apportionment | A statutory fallback under which mandatory health funds are treated as apportioned or otherwise available when ordinary executive apportionment action is delayed or withheld. |

| Derived value | A quantity calculated from other inputs by a stated equation rather than entered independently as an assumption, target, or observed datum. |

| Diagnostic-first pathway | A specialist-access pathway that completes defined diagnostic work before or in parallel with specialist review when doing so is safe, appropriate, and unlikely to delay urgent care. |

| Diagnostic-treatment unit | A community-based Type A, B, C, or D service unit that provides protocolized assessment, diagnostics, treatment, follow-up, escalation, and record integration within its certified scope. |

| E-consult | An asynchronous clinician-to-specialist consultation based on a structured clinical question and referral packet that may resolve the issue, recommend further workup, or authorize escalation. |

| Essential service line | A hospital or regional service whose loss would materially impair emergency, maternal, psychiatric, pediatric, trauma, intensive, rural, dialysis, stroke, cardiac, safety-net, or other required population capability. |

| Externally sourced data | An empirical value drawn from an identified external source, with citation, reference period, population, method, and transformation recorded. |

| Failure mode | A specific way an element, function, interface, policy, transition action, or external condition can fail to produce its intended result. |

| Federated public infrastructure | A governed network of interoperable services and records in which authority, access, computation, and storage may be distributed while standards, rights, auditability, and public accountability remain national. |

| Final framework assumption | A controlling design or quantitative premise adopted for the current framework version. It remains a model assumption unless independently supported as an external fact. |

| First-decade transition-adjusted annual cost | The average or representative annual total-system cost during the initial transition decade after adding incremental transition and implementation costs and accounting for the timing of operating changes. Current framework assumption: approximately $4.90T–$5.05T per year in 2024 dollars. |

| Formula Registry | The controlled, public, versioned registry of formulas affecting payment, access, benefits, routing, workforce allocation, priority, reserves, or other material rights and resources. |

| Four-unit diagnostic-treatment network | The National Community Diagnostic and Treatment Network composed of Type A Micro-Units, Type B Standard Neighborhood Diagnostic and Treatment Units, Type C Rural Enhanced Units, and Type D Urban/Public Health Units. |

| Global budget | A prospective public operating allocation for a hospital or defined facility scope, adjusted through transparent formulas for population need, case mix, readiness, service-line obligations, staffing safety, capital interfaces, and regional access. |

| High-stakes decision | A decision that can deny, terminate, delay, materially reduce, or fail to escalate care, coverage, benefits, payment, long-term care, urgent referral, or another protected health interest. |

| Human-accountable AI | Use of AI for assistance, prediction, prioritization, documentation, or routing in which a qualified human or legally accountable body retains responsibility, can review and override the result, and leaves an auditable decision record. |

| Implementation phase | A controlled time-bounded stage PH-P0 through PH-P8 that introduces specified capabilities and may advance only when applicable readiness gates are independently satisfied. |

| Independent verification | Verification performed or certified by a body institutionally separate from the element responsible for producing the measured performance. |

| Information Mesh | The National Health Assurance Information Mesh: federated public infrastructure for identity, longitudinal records, coverage and claims, rules-as-code, capacity and supply ledgers, workforce data, quality and safety, appeals, research, cybersecurity, and public transparency. |

| Interface | A defined exchange, dependency, authority boundary, or flow between architecture elements, including information, funds, decisions, services, products, people, legal authority, or verification evidence. |

| Key Performance Parameter | A small set of outcome-oriented parameters whose failure would materially undermine framework success and that therefore receive senior governance attention, independent verification, and phase-gate linkage where applicable. |

| Layer 3 — Transition protection | The temporary and staged protections that preserve patient care, medication access, provider liquidity, hospital services, pharmacy operation, records, workforce pathways, and intergovernmental continuity during migration. |

| Layer 4 — Legitimacy and safety | The durable rights, safety, privacy, transparency, usability, equity, appeal, ombudsman, diagnostic-safety, and human-accountability protections needed for trustworthy operation. |

| Layer 5 — Adaptation and repair | The durable scorekeeping, formula control, retrospective review, sunset, red-team, legal-contingency, corrective-action, technology-lifecycle, and evidence-based repair functions. |

| Legacy payer | A private or public coverage or claims entity whose pretransition obligations, data, appeals, liabilities, and payment runout must be transferred, reconciled, or wound down. |

| Legitimacy | The condition in which system authority and decisions are understandable, procedurally fair, reviewable, rights-respecting, evidence-linked, publicly accountable, and sufficiently trusted for durable operation. |

| Mature steady state | The postimplementation operating condition following Phase 8 maturity certification, when core capabilities, benefits, financing, reserves, workforce, oversight, and data systems meet defined requirements. |

| Model parameter | A named, typed, unit-bearing simulation input with a central value or distribution, provenance, dimensionality, uncertainty treatment, and scenario behavior. |

| National Health Assurance | The proposed national public entitlement and operating system that provides public default coverage, finances covered medically necessary care, organizes delivery capacity, and governs payment, information, rights, transition, and adaptation. |

| National Health Assurance Trust | The source-package term for the mandatory entitlement financing and payment-authorization structure. Its legal and accounting relationship to the National Health Equalization Trust Fund must be resolved before the financing sections are baselined. |

| National Health Equalization Trust Fund | The framework's operating stabilization, shock and transition reserve, and permanent health-endowment structure. It is distinct from ordinary annual program operations, subject to the financing-role clarification noted above. |

| No balance billing | A prohibition on a participating provider or facility billing a covered person beyond the authorized patient amount for covered care. |

| No Silent Rationing Doctrine | The rule that access constraints, denials, non-referrals, benefit limits, priority rules, and resource-allocation decisions may not be hidden; affected persons must receive the governing reason, evidence or rule, responsible human authority, alternatives, and appeal path. |

| Open issue | A material question not resolved by the authoritative source. Open issues are recorded explicitly and may not be filled with invented precision. |

| Ordinary household | A household outside the high-income, extreme-wealth, or other specifically targeted progressive financing bases; the exact statutory thresholds remain to be defined. |

| Phase gate | An independently verified decision point that blocks or permits implementation progression based on defined entry criteria, performance thresholds, risk status, legal readiness, and corrective-action closure. |

| Plausible range | A bounded model-assumption interval intended to represent reasonable uncertainty or scenario variation, not a statistical confidence interval unless a statistical method is stated. |

| Point-of-care cost | A patient payment demanded when receiving, scheduling, filling, or accessing covered care, including applicable copayments, coinsurance, deductibles, or balance bills; it does not mean that the care has no economic cost to the system. |

| Primary care | Longitudinal clinical care emphasizing continuity, complexity, multimorbidity, frailty, disability, family context, prevention, chronic-disease management, and goals of care, distinct from but connected to unit-based low-acuity access. |

| Protected urgent specialist slot | Specialist capacity reserved from ordinary scheduling for urgency-class referrals or related protected functions, including designated e-consult work. |

| Provisional coverage | Immediate temporary coverage applied when eligibility or migration information is unresolved so that administrative uncertainty does not interrupt medically necessary care. |

| Provisional payment | A temporary Treasury or public payment issued when a qualifying clean claim or transition obligation misses its statutory deadline, followed by controlled reconciliation. |

| Public budget cost | Government outlays and public administrative costs attributable to the framework. It is not interchangeable with total-system cost because residual private and patient-paid spending may remain. |

| Public default coverage | Automatic enrollment into the public core coverage system for eligible people unless a legally permitted and certified alternative applies; loss or absence of private coverage does not create a coverage gap. |

| Public-service hospital charter | A binding public payment and governance instrument that conditions hospital participation and funding on essential-service, access, staffing, reporting, anti-extraction, and continuity obligations. |

| Regional Health Administrator | The regional operating authority responsible for capacity planning and execution across units, hospitals, specialty queues, EMS, public health, and approved local adaptation. |

| Requirement | A uniquely identified, traceable, verifiable statement of an obligatory project or system outcome expressed with 'shall.' |

| Residual private spending | Health spending that remains outside public outlays after implementation, including permitted supplemental care, certified private roles, and noncovered services. |

| Risk | An uncertain event or condition that may affect cost, schedule, access, safety, quality, equity, legality, legitimacy, continuity, or other framework objectives. |

| Rules-as-code | A version-controlled, testable, human-readable and machine-executable representation of benefit, payment, formulary, routing, appeal, formula, or other operational rules, with legal authority and audit history preserved. |

| Scenario | A coherent set of parameter changes, events, implementation conditions, or shocks applied to both the framework and comparator where relevant. |

| Secure Research and Analytics Enclave | A controlled environment for privacy-preserving research, evaluation, simulation calibration, and analytics with governed access, disclosure controls, and auditability. |

| Sensitivity analysis | Systematic variation of inputs or structural assumptions to estimate their influence on outputs and identify thresholds, nonlinearities, or dominant uncertainties. |

| Specialist Bottleneck Index | A composite performance measure of constrained specialist capacity. Its component specialties, weights, normalization, and baseline require formal specification before use. |

| Specialist routing backplane | The coordinated national-regional infrastructure that uses structured referral packets, urgency classes, e-consults, tele-specialty, diagnostic-first pathways, capacity ledgers, protected slots, patient constraints, and closed-loop follow-up to allocate specialty access. |

| Stakeholder need | A solution-neutral statement of an outcome a stakeholder requires or values. Top-level needs use SN identifiers and may be decomposed into derived needs. |

| State variable | A modeled quantity that describes the system at a point in time and changes through transition rules, flows, events, or feedback. |

| Supplemental private coverage | Certified private coverage for services or amenities outside the public core benefit that may not reduce public rights, delay public access, or shift covered obligations to patients. |

| System cost | The total economic health-system spending within the defined boundary, regardless of whether paid by government, employers, households, or residual private arrangements. |

| Target | A required or desired value for a parameter at a stated phase, time, population, and scope. A target is neither an observed baseline nor a forecast unless separately identified. |

| Technical Performance Parameter | A measurable performance characteristic of a subsystem, process, interface, or enabling capability used to monitor design and implementation performance. |

| Tele-specialty | Synchronous or asynchronous specialist care delivered remotely when clinically appropriate, with the same routing, documentation, privacy, safety, and follow-up obligations as other specialist pathways. |

| Total-system cost | Public outlays plus residual private spending and patient-paid health spending within the stated scope and year. Current mature central framework assumption: approximately $4.75T per year in 2024 dollars. |

| Transition and implementation cost | Incremental time-limited spending required to create infrastructure, expand capacity, stabilize participants, migrate data and coverage, retrain workers, and protect continuity. Current framework assumption: $1.2T–$2.0T over 10–12 years. |

| Type A Micro-Unit | The smallest certified diagnostic-treatment unit, designed for geographically distributed access to a limited low-acuity, screening, testing, treatment, and follow-up scope. |

| Type B Standard Neighborhood Diagnostic and Treatment Unit | The standard community unit providing broader routine diagnostic-treatment capability, protocolized low-acuity care, chronic monitoring, follow-up, and escalation. |

| Type C Rural Enhanced Unit | A rural or frontier unit with enhanced diagnostics, stabilization, observation, tele-specialty, transport coordination, and escalation capability tailored to distance and sparse capacity. |

| Type D Urban/Public Health Unit | An urban unit combining high-throughput diagnostic-treatment access with public-health, surveillance, prevention, outreach, and surge functions. |

| Uncertainty distribution | A documented probability distribution or bounded sampling rule used when a parameter cannot responsibly be represented by a single value. |

| Urgency class | A standardized referral or appeal priority category with defined clinical criteria, maximum response time, scheduling rule, escalation path, and verification timestamps. |

| Validation | Evidence that the model, rule, measure, or system is fit for its intended use and adequately represents the relevant real-world or policy construct. |

| Verification | Objective evidence that a requirement, calculation, interface, rule, or implementation product satisfies its specified criteria. |

| Verification requirement | A requirement governing the evidence, method, independence, population, records, thresholds, and pass/fail criteria used to verify other requirements. |

| Volatile revenue exposure | The portion of required financing expected to vary materially with asset values, income realization, business cycles, litigation, compliance, or other uncertainty and therefore used to size stabilization reserves. |

| Wage pass-through | The required conversion of employer health-benefit savings or obligations during transition into worker compensation or another specified worker benefit, measured against an auditable baseline. |
Traceability and ID Convention
Traceability purpose
Traceability is the mechanism by which a policy rationale becomes an implementable, verifiable, and simulatable system specification. Each controlled object has one permanent ID, an object type, an owner or responsible element where applicable, a status, a source basis, and explicit relationships to upstream needs and downstream implementation or evidence.
Table D1-8. Controlled identifier families

| Family | Canonical pattern | Object | Example | Control rule |

| ASM | ASM-### | Design, evaluation, or modeling assumption | ASM-001 | Retained with status and version; never silently converted into fact. |

| SN | SN-## | Top-level stakeholder need | SN-01 | Solution-neutral outcome; derived needs trace upward. |

| PR | PR-<domain>-### | Project requirement | PR-CST-001 | Controls implementation cost, schedule, workforce, or transition outcomes. |

| SR | SR-<domain>-### | System requirement | SR-COV-001 | Defines required operational or architectural behavior. |

| VR | VR-### | Verification requirement | VR-001 | Defines evidence, method, independence, and pass/fail discipline. |

| KPP | KPP-<domain><n> | Key Performance Parameter | KPP-B5 | Outcome-critical parameter; may control phase progression. |

| TPP | TPP-<domain>.<n> or named suffix | Technical Performance Parameter | TPP-7.2 / TPP-EMP1 | Subsystem or enabling performance measure. |

| CP | CP-<category>-### | Cost parameter | CP-HOSP-001 | Typed and unit-bearing; category remains stable across model versions. |

| ARCH | ARCH-<mnemonic> | Architecture element | ARCH-DNHA | Unique responsible institution, office, fund, court, or network. |

| IF | IF-### | Standalone interface-catalog record | IF-001 | Reserved for Appendix I; current interface requirements remain SR-IF-###. |

| PH | PH-P# | Implementation phase | PH-P6 | P0–P8 roadmap with explicit year and gate relationships. |

| RISK | RISK-<domain>-### | Risk or failure mode | RISK-SPEC-001 | Links warning indicators, mitigations, owners, recovery, and verification. |

| SCN | SCN-<mnemonic> | Simulation scenario | SCN-CYBER | Defines coherent parameter/event changes and comparator treatment. |
Identity, lifecycle, and status rules
One ID identifies one semantic object. The same statement may not receive multiple IDs merely because it appears in multiple sections.
IDs are never recycled. Rejected and superseded objects remain in the controlled register with status and rationale.
Editorial renaming that does not change meaning retains the ID and records an alias. A material semantic change requires a new version and may require a new ID.
Canonical status values are Draft, Proposed, Baselined, Verified, Superseded, Rejected, Retired, and Open. 'Final' identifies a controlled integrated release; this public-explanatory baseline is version 2.0.0.
References use full IDs. Ranges such as SN-01–SN-25 may summarize a set but may not substitute for object-level links in a machine-readable matrix.
Every object record carries source authority and version. The current directive and source package are the initial framework authorities; external evidence is separately identified.
Requirement construction
Project and system requirements use the syntax: [responsible project or system] shall [single necessary action or outcome] [measurable performance] [applicable conditions and phase/time] [without embedding implementation detail unless the detail is itself required]. Each requirement has a verification method and bidirectional links to at least one need, parent requirement, parameter, architecture element, risk, statute, or interface as applicable.
Table D1-9. Permitted primary verification methods

| Method | Use |

| Inspection | Review of documents, configuration, authority, records, physical presence, or controlled artifacts. |

| Analysis | Calculation, statistical evaluation, model output, audited data analysis, or logical proof. |

| Test | Controlled stimulus with measured response and explicit pass/fail criteria. |

| Demonstration | Execution of an operational scenario with entry criteria, observed outputs, exit criteria, and pass/fail determination. |
Required relationship model
Table D1-10. Core trace relationships

| Relationship | From | To | Meaning |

| derives | SN or requirement | Derived need or child requirement | The downstream object decomposes an upstream outcome without changing its intent. |

| satisfies | PR/SR | SN | The requirement contributes objective evidence that a stakeholder need is met. |

| allocated_to | PR/SR/VR/KPP/TPP/RISK | ARCH | The architecture element owns or supports implementation, measurement, mitigation, or verification. |

| measured_by | SN/PR/SR | KPP/TPP | The parameter operationalizes satisfaction or performance. |

| costed_by | ARCH/function/requirement | CP | The cost parameter represents an attributable resource or offset. |

| exchanged_through | ARCH/function | IF | The object depends on a controlled information, fund, authority, service, or product interface. |

| implemented_in | PR/SR/ARCH | PH | The object is established, scaled, or certified in the phase. |

| threatened_by | SN/PR/SR/ARCH | RISK | The risk may impair satisfaction or operation. |

| verified_by | PR/SR/KPP/TPP/PH gate | VR/evidence record | The evidence and method determine compliance or readiness. |

| exercised_in | ARCH/IF/RISK/CP | SCN | The scenario varies or stresses the object in simulation. |
INTERFACE CONTROL  The source package currently expresses interface dependencies as SR-IF-001 through SR-IF-015. The standalone IF-### family is reserved for the Appendix I catalog. Appendix I maps each SR-IF requirement to one or more IF records without renaming the requirements.
Minimum controlled-object metadata
ID, object type, canonical name, concise statement, status, version, and source authority.
Owner, supporting elements, verifier, applicable phase, and decision authority where relevant.
Upstream and downstream trace links, including rationale for any intentionally absent relationship.
For quantitative objects: definition, equation, unit, denominator, dimensions, baseline, target, range/distribution, and update frequency.
For requirements and gates: verification method, evidence source, pass/fail rule, and independent verification responsibility.
For risks: causes, effects, early warnings, mitigations, fallback, recovery objective, residual risk, and linked scenarios.
Simulation-Readiness Convention
Purpose and boundary
Simulation readiness means that another AI or software agent can distinguish designed policy, required performance, observed comparator data, uncertain model inputs, calculated values, and unresolved questions without inferring meaning from prose alone. It does not mean that every parameter is already calibrated or that the document itself is executable code.
Table D1-11. Quantitative statement classifications

| Class | Label | Meaning | Required metadata |

| FA | Final framework assumption | Controlling framework premise or cost position used unless a controlled revision changes it. | Source version, value/range, unit, price year, scope, rationale, sensitivity. |

| MP | Model parameter | Typed simulation input that may vary by scenario, time, geography, or population. | ID, data type, unit, dimensions, central value/distribution, provenance, scenario behavior. |

| TG | Target | Desired or required future performance at a stated phase or time. | KPP/TPP or requirement link, numerator, denominator, scope, deadline, verification. |

| ED | Externally sourced data | Observed or estimated empirical value imported from a cited source. | Citation, source date, reference period, population, method, transformation, uncertainty. |

| DV | Derived value | Value calculated from other controlled inputs. | Equation, input IDs and versions, unit checks, rounding, reproducibility record. |

| OI | Open issue | Value or definition not responsibly resolved. | Question, decision owner, needed evidence, downstream impact, closure criterion. |
Canonical machine-usable record
Table D1-12. Minimum simulation-record fields

| Field | Purpose |

| id / object_type / version / status | Stable identity and lifecycle control. |

| name / definition / statement | Human-readable semantic content. |

| source_class / source_authority / citation | Distinguishes framework authority, model choice, and external evidence. |

| owner_arch_id / verifier_arch_id | Assigns operation, measurement, and independent assurance. |

| unit / currency_year / data_type | Prevents unit and price-basis ambiguity. |

| dimensions | Declares applicable time, geography, population, service, facility, product, agency, and scenario axes. |

| baseline / central / minimum / maximum / distribution | Separates observed baseline, central assumption, bounds, and probabilistic uncertainty. |

| target / target_phase / tolerance | Represents required or desired performance independently from forecast output. |

| equation / dependencies / trace_links | Supports calculation, causal structure, allocation, and reproducibility. |

| verification_method / evidence_record / quality_flags | Supports validation, phase-gate use, and data-quality controls. |

| scenario_overrides / sensitivity_range | Defines controlled variation without changing the baseline object. |

| notes / open_issue_link | Preserves bounded interpretation and unresolved decisions. |
Units, dimensions, and missing values
Currency values use real 2024 U.S. dollars unless a record explicitly states another price basis. Nominal conversions must identify the deflator and source.
Percent and percentage point are distinct units. Ratios, rates, counts, time intervals, and index values must state denominators and observation windows.
Minimum dimensions are time/phase, geography/jurisdiction, population group, service category, unit type, specialty, hospital/service line, product category, owning agency, and scenario where applicable.
Unknown, not applicable, suppressed, and not yet calibrated are distinct states. None may be encoded as numeric zero.
Ranges must state whether they are plausible bounds, legal limits, engineering tolerances, statistical intervals, or sampled distributions.
Every parameter transformation preserves the source value and records the equation, input versions, rounding, and unit conversion.
Comparator symmetry and causal discipline
The framework and existing-system comparator use aligned population, economic, time, service, and outcome boundaries unless a documented reason requires asymmetry.
Policy targets are not hard-coded as achieved outcomes. The model produces outcomes from capacity, behavior, financing, transition, and feedback assumptions.
Cost offsets require an explicit causal pathway, lag, attribution rule, uncertainty range, and prevention of double counting.
Capacity constraints, queues, induced utilization, workforce limits, regional heterogeneity, and transition failures must be represented rather than assumed away.
Legal, cyber, supply, trust, and governance failures enter through scenarios or state transitions with defined recovery behavior.
Calibration, verification, and reproducibility
Calibration data and validation data are separated where feasible.
Parameter sets, source extracts, equations, code, random seeds, and scenario overrides are versioned as a reproducible model release.
Each output traces to the state variables, parameters, equations, and scenarios that produced it.
Phase-gate measures require independent verification before they can permit implementation progression.
Sensitivity, threshold, uncertainty, and structural-alternative analyses accompany central results.
The simulation reports confidence and limitations; it does not convert unresolved policy questions into hidden defaults.

1. Purpose
PART DECISION QUESTION  What public purpose must the framework serve, what mature system state is intended, and how will success be judged without confusing targets with achieved outcomes?
1.1 Purpose of the Framework
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: A national redesign can accumulate programs without a stable public purpose; the framework therefore needs a single statement of the outcomes every later component must serve. Why this structure: Purpose is kept above design so later architecture can be rejected when it does not serve the declared end state. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes purpose of the framework explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Define the national policy purpose, the systems-engineering purpose, and the simulation purpose of National Health Assurance. |

| System entities | Congress; DNHA; NHAC; NBIA; THDO; NHETF; NHTCA; NHASB; CHAO; Article I court; RHAs; state, regional, and tribal partners; providers and public utilities. |

| Assumptions | ASM-003, ASM-006, ASM-009–ASM-015, ASM-018, ASM-029, ASM-034–035. |

| Data / parameters | SN-01–SN-25; CP-TOT/POP/FIN; comparator record set; KPP/TPP definitions. |

| Requirements / performance | PR-CST, PR-SCH, PR-WF, PR-TRN; all core SR families; KPP-A/B/C/D/E/T/W/TRUST. |

| Principal risks | Purpose drift; benefit creep; target-as-outcome error; fiscal boundary confusion; exclusion of underserved groups. |

| Simulation implication | Purpose defines the objective vector and constraints. It does not supply parameter values or guarantee performance. |
National Health Assurance exists to provide a durable public guarantee of access to covered medically necessary care while shifting financial risk away from illness, employment status, and fragmented payer rules. It is intended to make core coverage continuous, patient cost at the point of care zero or near zero, payment predictable, capacity visible and managed, safety independently auditable, and institutional repair possible without making the system easy to sabotage.
The framework is not only a coverage statute. It is a coordinated operating system: entitlement and financing authorities, care-delivery networks, claims and pharmacy utilities, hospital public-service arrangements, workforce pipelines, information infrastructure, rights and appeals, transition safeguards, and adaptation mechanisms must function together. A coverage promise without capacity, records, payment, or continuity would fail the purpose.
Purpose layers

| Layer | Purpose | Decision consequence |

| Public-policy purpose | Protect residents from avoidable financial harm and discontinuous access while preserving safety, quality, equity, innovation, and fiscal sustainability. | Benefits, financing, rights, and capacity are evaluated together. |

| Operational purpose | Replace fragmented core payment and routing with public default coverage, common rails, managed capacity, and accountable regional delivery. | Architecture must allocate every critical function and failure fallback. |

| Transition purpose | Move patients, providers, workers, employers, plans, records, and cash flows without preventable treatment or payment interruption. | Layer 3 is a primary system layer and transition cost is explicit. |

| Legitimacy and safety purpose | Make decisions explainable, human-accountable, appealable, privacy-preserving, and independently visible. | Layer 4 is funded and measured, not treated as communications overhead. |

| Adaptation purpose | Correct formulas, rules, technology, and organization through evidence and bounded authority. | Layer 5 includes review, sunset, rollback, and anti-sabotage controls. |

| Simulation purpose | Permit transparent comparison with the existing U.S. system under common populations, shocks, time, and accounting boundaries. | All assumptions, targets, data, equations, and uncertainty remain distinguishable. |
What the purpose does not authorize
It does not imply that care has zero economic cost or that demand and capacity are unconstrained.
It does not convert every social determinant into a covered healthcare benefit; clinically linked supports require a controlled nexus.
It does not assign high-stakes clinical or benefit decisions to autonomous AI.
It does not treat private residual roles, state responsibilities, tribal sovereignty, or local adaptation as undefined exceptions.
It does not claim that the $4.75T central cost assumption has already been empirically validated.
1.2 Desired End State
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Readers and implementers need to know what daily care, payment, rights, and governance should look like when the transition is complete. Why this structure: Purpose is kept above design so later architecture can be rejected when it does not serve the declared end state. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes desired end state explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Specify the mature configuration and behaviors that define completion without prescribing every implementation detail. |

| System entities | All final framework institutions and operating domains, including Type A–D units, specialist backplane, hospitals, medicines, workforce, information, transition, legitimacy/safety, and adaptation bodies. |

| Assumptions | ASM-003–ASM-014, ASM-018, ASM-021–ASM-025, ASM-030–ASM-031. |

| Data / parameters | Mature KPP/TPP values, state variables, capacity ledgers, cost ledgers, service and rights records. |

| Requirements / performance | SR-ARCH, SR-COV, SR-ACC, SR-SPEC, SR-PAY, SR-DRUG, SR-HOSP, SR-LTC/BH/DVH/EMS, SR-DATA, SR-LAW, SR-ADP. |

| Principal risks | Nominal compliance without real capacity; regional inequity; fiscal underfunding; brittle centralization; hidden residual billing. |

| Simulation implication | The end state initializes the framework maturity scenario and supplies terminal constraints for phase-gate evaluation. |
At maturity, an eligible resident is in public default coverage without relying on a job, annual reenrollment, or a commercial risk-selection decision. A request for care enters through an appropriate local, virtual, emergency, or specialty pathway; identity, coverage, relevant records, and follow-up ownership persist across settings. Covered medically necessary care normally generates no patient bill at the point of care.
Care capacity is managed rather than assumed. Type A–D diagnostic-treatment units provide a broad front door; structured referral packets, urgency classes, e-consults, tele-specialty, diagnostic-first pathways, regional capacity ledgers, and protected urgent slots manage specialty demand. Hospitals operate under public-service charters and separated operating, readiness, and capital budgets. Essential services and safe staffing constrain savings.
Core claims, pharmacy payment, drug purchasing, public manufacturing backup, provider/facility registries, and a federated Information Mesh operate as public infrastructure. AI supports documentation, prediction, routing, and review, but accountable humans retain specified high-stakes authority. Independent bodies measure performance, hear complaints, verify safety, score fiscal and operational results, and provide enforceable remedies.
Table D2-4. Mature end-state dimensions

| Dimension | Mature-state condition | Observable state |

| Coverage and rights | Automatic public default coverage; provisional coverage for unresolved status; understandable notices and appeals. | Coverage state, termination reason, notice, appeal, remedy |

| Benefit and price | Covered medically necessary care and essential formulary services at zero or near-zero point-of-care cost. | Benefit class, patient charge, exception, noncovered/residual ledger |

| Front-door care | Type A–D units and mobile equivalents meet geographic and same-day access standards. | Unit count/type, travel time, request and resolution time, escalation |

| Specialty access | Every nonemergency referral has a complete packet, urgency class, queue position, and follow-up owner. | Specialty-region queue, protected capacity, response and completion |

| Hospitals | Global operating budgets and charters preserve essential services, readiness, staffing, and capital stewardship. | Budget components, variance, service continuity, staffing, capital |

| Medicines and supply | National purchasing, public claims, transparent formulary, shortage surveillance, and public/dual-source backup. | Price, fill, inventory, source, shortage, substitution, appeal |

| Workforce | Training, compensation, scope, service obligations, and regional deployment align workforce supply with need. | Workforce stock, vacancies, workload, pipeline, retention, geography |

| Information and AI | Federated identity/record services, patient rights, auditability, resilience, and human-accountable AI. | Record availability, corrections, access log, uptime, model registry, override |

| Finance | Dedicated revenue covers certified obligations; reserves protect volatile receipts and shocks; burdens are distributionally visible. | Receipts, outlays, obligations, reserves, incidence, shortfall triggers |

| Governance and repair | Operational, rights/safety, scorekeeping, legislative-audit, judicial, regional, and tribal roles are explicit. | Decision owner, verifier, publication, appeal, review, sunset, rollback |
MATURITY IS CONDITIONAL  Phase 8 is not reached because a date passes. It is reached only when applicable gates and independent verification show that required capability, safety, access, continuity, financing, and accountability conditions have been satisfied.
1.3 Success Definition
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Coverage legislation can be declared successful while care remains inaccessible, unaffordable, or unsafe unless success is defined in observable terms. Why this structure: Purpose is kept above design so later architecture can be rejected when it does not serve the declared end state. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes success definition explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Translate stakeholder needs into measurable success conditions while preserving target, baseline, and observed-result distinctions. |

| System entities | Patients, providers, facilities, workforce, employers, states/regions/tribal nations, financing bodies, oversight bodies, innovators, and simulation builders. |

| Assumptions | ASM-015, ASM-030, ASM-032–ASM-035. |

| Data / parameters | SN-01–SN-25; KPP/TPP; uncertainty, equity, verification, and evidence records. |

| Requirements / performance | Every outcome-bearing PR/SR and VR-001–VR-015. |

| Principal risks | Metric gaming; aggregate success hiding subgroup failure; unverified self-report; target clipping; confidence omitted. |

| Simulation implication | Simulation produces outcomes and requirement results by phase and subgroup; it may report partial, failed, or indeterminate success. |
SUCCESS RULE  success = capability ∩ access ∩ safety ∩ continuity ∩ equity ∩ fiscal sufficiency ∩ rights/legitimacy
No single cost or coverage measure substitutes for the multidimensional result. Required gates and safety constraints are conjunctive unless the governing requirement explicitly says otherwise.
Success is defined from the perspective of affected stakeholders and then verified as system performance. A target is a desired or required threshold. It is not evidence that the threshold has been achieved. The final model must report the measured value, uncertainty, population, time, verifier, and status for each KPP or TPP.
Table D2-5. Stakeholder success matrix

| Need | Stakeholder | Success condition | Primary measure | Class |

| SN-01 | Patients / households | Covered care is financially non-ruinous | KPP-A3 covered-billing rate ≤0.5%; KPP-A4 medical-debt incidence ≤1% of baseline | TG |

| SN-02 | Eligible residents | Core coverage is continuous across life and employment changes | KPP-A1 continuous coverage ≥99.5%; KPP-A2 residual uninsured ≤0.2% | TG |

| SN-03 | Patients / communities | Common care is available promptly near home | KPP-B2 same-day low-acuity access ≥85%; KPP-B7 access-standard coverage ≥95% | TG |

| SN-04 | Patients / specialists | Clinically warranted specialist care is timely | KPP-B5 routine median wait ≤30 days; KPP-B6 urgent timeliness ≥95% | TG |

| SN-05 | Patients in transition | Treatment, medications, referrals, and plans survive migration | KPP-T1 active-treatment transfer ≥99%; KPP-T2 critical medication interruption ≤0.2% | TG |

| SN-06 | Providers | Covered services produce predictable, timely payment | TPP-2.2 clean-claim timeliness ≥99%; provisional Treasury payment when rails fail | TG |

| SN-07 | Hospitals / communities | Essential service lines remain available | TPP-5.4 essential-service continuity ≥95% of regions | TG |

| SN-08 | Patients / pharmacies | Essential medicines are reliably available | TPP-3.5 critical-shortage exposure ≤3%; TPP-3.2 essential $0 fills ≥98% | TG |

| SN-09 | Health workforce | Compensation, workload, safety, and careers are sustainable | TPP-8.1 critical vacancy ≤5%; safety-culture and burnout measures | TG/OI |

| SN-10 | Displaced administrative workers | Transition pathways prevent avoidable dislocation | KPP-W1 placement or training ≥75% | TG |

| SN-11 | Sponsors / funders | Obligations are sustainably and transparently financed | KPP-C5 dedicated revenue sufficiency ≥100%; KPP-C6 reserve adequacy ≥12 months | TG |

| SN-12 | Ordinary households | They do not become the fallback financing source | KPP-C8 incremental ordinary-household burden share ≤5% | TG |

| SN-13 | Implementers / public | Core functions withstand nonfeasance and sabotage | TPP-12.1 mandatory-payment protection ≥99.5%; TPP-2.5 protected disbursement ≥99.8% | TG |

| SN-14 | Patients / providers | Decisions are explained, reviewable, and appealable | TPP-LEG1 explanation completeness ≥98%; appeal timeliness and urgent relief | TG/OI |

| SN-15 | Patients / data stewards | Records are accessible, correctable, private, and auditable | TPP-10.5 correction closure ≥97%; sensitive-access audits ≥99% | TG |

| SN-16 | Patients / safety bodies | Diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up are reliably closed loop | TPP-6.3 abnormal-result closure ≥99%; KPP-B9 unsafe under-referral ≤3/10,000 | TG |

| SN-17 | AI-affected stakeholders | AI is safe, auditable, nondiscriminatory, and human-accountable | TPP-11.5 high-stakes human-review capture ≥99% | TG |

| SN-18 | Underserved groups | Access, quality, safety, and outcomes are equitable | KPP-E1 coverage gap ≤0.5 pp; KPP-E3 specialist-wait ratio ≤1.10 | TG |

| SN-19 | Patients / navigators | Services, rights, and appeals are usable | TPP-USE1 rights comprehension ≥90%; TPP-USE2 unassisted appeal completion ≥85% | TG |

| SN-20 | Public / oversight | Performance and conflicts are visible | TPP-12.4 required publication timeliness ≥99%; public trust measure | TG/OI |

| SN-21 | Framework stewards | The system repairs defects without becoming easy to sabotage | Required review and sunset completion ≥99%; corrective-action closure | TG/OI |

| SN-22 | Patients / innovators | Valuable innovation continues without monopoly pricing as default | TPP-13.1 active public programs in ≥95% priority unmet-need areas | TG |

| SN-23 | Regions / states | Local adaptation coexists with national standards | TPP-REG1 evaluated adaptation waivers ≥95% | TG |

| SN-24 | Tribal nations | Integration preserves sovereignty and federal trust duties | TPP-TRIB1 compact execution/compliance ≥98% | TG |

| SN-25 | Employers / workers | Core-benefit transition is predictable and reaches wages | TPP-EMP1 wage-pass-through compliance ≥95% | TG |
Success decision logic
Compute each measure from observed or simulated events; do not overwrite the result with its target.
Apply denominator, time, geography, service, and population definitions before comparison with a threshold.
Report national performance together with prespecified equity strata and regional distributions.
Require the verification method and evidence source stated in the linked VR or requirement record.
Return Pass, Fail, Indeterminate, or Not Applicable. Missing evidence cannot produce Pass.
If a phase gate fails, hold or revert the dependent capability and execute the specified recovery or fallback pathway.
Section 1 CONCLUSION  The framework's purpose is a public assurance of financially protected, continuous, capacity-supported, safe, equitable, and accountable care. Its desired end state is an integrated operating system, not an insurance card. Success is measured across all SN-01–SN-25 outcomes and may not be declared from aggregate cost or coverage alone.
2. Problems
PART DECISION QUESTION  What existing-system mechanisms produce the outcomes the framework is intended to change, and what empirical baseline can be initialized without mixing survey concepts, years, forecasts, and framework targets?
2.1 Current U.S. Health-System Problem Statement
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: The current system's failures arise from interacting financing, access, administrative, market-power, and accountability mechanisms rather than from one isolated defect. Why this structure: Problem statements remain separate from preferred solutions so the comparison does not assume that the framework is the only possible remedy. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes current u.s. health-system problem statement explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Define the current-system problem as interacting mechanisms rather than a list of undesirable outcomes. |

| System entities | Federal and state programs; private plans and PBMs; employers; patients; providers; hospitals; pharmacies; manufacturers; vendors; regulators; courts; public-health and emergency systems. |

| Assumptions | ASM-016, ASM-020, ASM-023–ASM-024, ASM-029, ASM-031. |

| Data / parameters | T-ED-001–T-ED-018; baseline record keys; KPP/TPP baseline fields; regional and distributional dimensions. |

| Requirements / performance | PR-CST-001; inverse conditions of SN-01–SN-25; RISK-BASE-* taxonomy. |

| Principal risks | Causal overclaim; stale evidence; national-average masking; assuming all actors fail in the same way; treating reform targets as baseline facts. |

| Simulation implication | Failure mechanisms become comparator rules, shocks, queues, costs, and transition conditions—not hard-coded claims that the framework performs better. |
The current U.S. health system is not one coherent system. It is an interacting set of public programs, employer-sponsored arrangements, commercial plans, provider organizations, benefit managers, vendors, regulators, and state rules. The same person may move among these arrangements or use several at once. Coverage, payment, records, referral authority, formulary access, and appeals can therefore change without a corresponding change in medical need.
This fragmentation does not imply that every institution or episode performs poorly. It means that system-level continuity, accountability, capacity allocation, and financial protection are emergent and uneven rather than guaranteed. The comparison must preserve existing strengths and progress—such as broad hospital electronic exchange—while measuring the gaps that remain.
Empirical anchors
CMS reports 2024 national health expenditure of $5.3 trillion, $15,474 per person, and 18.0% of GDP. Medicare, Medicaid, private health insurance, and out-of-pocket spending accounted for 21%, 18%, 31%, and 11% of NHE, respectively. These are observed external data, not framework assumptions. [T-ED-001]
The Census Bureau estimates that 27.1 million people, or 8.0%, were uninsured for all of 2024 under the CPS ASEC annual concept; 66.1% had private coverage and 35.5% had public coverage during the year, with overlap possible. State ACS uninsured rates ranged from 2.8% to 16.7%, demonstrating that a national mean is not an adequate regional initializer. [T-ED-002] [T-ED-003]
Financial exposure persists beyond the uninsured population. Census SIPP data indicate that about 16% of households held medical debt in 2023, with a $2,000 median balance. An older but still useful NCHS indicator found 10.8% of people lived in families reporting problems paying medical bills in 2021. The different unit, year, and concept prevent these measures from being combined into one rate. [T-ED-004] [T-ED-005]
Access and supply failures are heterogeneous. HRSA projects a shortage of 141,160 physician FTEs in 2038 under its assumptions; this is a forecast, not a 2024 observed count. GAO reports that at least 47% of physicians were consolidated with hospital systems in 2024 and that rural hospital closures increased travel distance for affected communities. These data support explicit market, workforce, and geography mechanisms rather than a single national capacity multiplier. [T-ED-008] [T-ED-009] [T-ED-010]
Interacting problem mechanisms

| Mechanism | System effect | Framework response tested later |

| Fragmented eligibility and payer rules | Coverage and authorizations can change at job, income, age, family, state, or plan transitions. | Public default and provisional coverage; continuity protections |

| Patient price exposure | Premiums, cost sharing, exclusions, and collections can delay care or create debt. | Zero/near-zero covered-care price; no balance billing; public financing |

| Administrative rule multiplicity | Clinicians and patients navigate different claims, prior-authorization, network, coding, and appeal requirements. | Common public rules and utilities; restricted authorization; explainable appeals |

| Unmanaged queues and local scarcity | Front-door and specialty access depend on uneven supply and opaque referral capacity. | Type A–D network; specialty ledgers, urgency classes, e-consults |

| Volume, site, and market incentives | Prices, facility fees, ownership, and extraction can diverge from community readiness and need. | Global budgets, charters, separated capital/readiness/service obligations |

| Incomplete benefit integration | LTC, behavioral health, dental, vision, hearing, EMS, and linked supports remain inconsistent. | Staged integrated benefit expansion with capacity gates |

| Data and vendor concentration | Records and payment rails may be incomplete, inaccessible, or vulnerable to common-mode outages. | Federated public mesh, continuity modes, public claims/pharmacy rails |

| Diffuse accountability | Responsibility for denials, pricing, access, safety, and repair is divided across institutions. | Independent accountability, scorekeeping, legislative audit, court remedies |
Prior authorization illustrates the need for balanced modeling. It may reduce some unnecessary utilization, but GAO reports stakeholder concerns about timely access and provider burden and cites an HHS OIG review in which 13% of sampled Medicare Advantage denials would have been covered in traditional Medicare. The simulation should therefore model both utilization-control value and delay/error cost rather than treat all authorization as either pure waste or pure benefit. [T-ED-011]
2.2 Existing-System Baseline for Comparison
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: A reform cannot be evaluated against an undefined status quo; cost, access, outcomes, rights, and capacity require a reproducible comparison baseline. Why this structure: Problem statements remain separate from preferred solutions so the comparison does not assume that the framework is the only possible remedy. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes existing-system baseline for comparison explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Create a reference-year and dynamic comparator that can initialize the simulation and support like-for-like comparison. |

| System entities | Existing federal/state programs, private coverage, employers, providers, facilities, manufacturers, households, and data authorities. |

| Assumptions | ASM-016–ASM-020, ASM-023, ASM-029–ASM-033. |

| Data / parameters | Baseline records in Table D2-7; CMS NHE and projections; Census coverage/population/debt; HRSA, GAO, ONC, FDA, SAMHSA, CDC evidence. |

| Requirements / performance | PR-CST-001; baseline fields for KPP-A/B/C/D/E and selected TPPs. |

| Principal risks | Concept mismatch; inconsistent denominators; stale values; projection-vintage drift; missing uncertainty; double counting payer shares. |

| Simulation implication | Initialize static C0 and dynamic C1 comparators; unresolved metrics remain explicit calibration tasks and receive sensitivity ranges only when justified. |
The comparator is the existing U.S. healthcare system as measured in a controlled reference state, not a rhetorical status quo. It has two required forms. Comparator C0 is a 2024 cross-sectional baseline used to align prices, population, spending, coverage, and selected capacity variables. Comparator C1 is a current-policy trajectory that evolves over the framework's 10–12-year transition horizon.
CMS projects average NHE growth of 5.4% from 2025 through 2034 versus 4.1% GDP growth, raising health spending from 18.0% to 20.6% of GDP. This is the macro anchor for C1, not a complete forecast for every service, payer, region, or population. Each submodule must retain its own source or calibrated rule. [T-ED-006]
Table D2-6. Comparator architecture

| Comparator | Purpose | Time treatment | Policy treatment | Use |

| C0 — Static 2024 | Common initialization and cross-sectional comparison | Observed source year retained; monetary values normalized to 2024 dollars | Policies and coverage as observed in 2024 | Baseline KPP/TPP values and cost reconciliation |

| C1 — Dynamic current policy | Counterfactual over the framework transition horizon | Annual 2025–2038 state path | Current-policy vintage plus enacted changes explicitly entered | Difference-in-outcomes and cumulative cost |

| C2 — Existing-system stress | Test resilience under shared shocks | Shock onset, duration, recovery | Existing architecture with shock-specific response | Cyber, recession, pandemic, supply, workforce, legal scenarios |

| F0/F1/F2 — Framework paths | Central, low/high, and transition/stress comparisons | PH-P0–PH-P8 and calendar years | Framework mechanisms and gate outcomes | Performance, risk, and distributional comparison |

Controlled cost reconciliation
The following calculations are derived values, not adopted targets. They use rounded public source values and therefore exist to expose denominator problems, not to create false precision.

| Derived record | Equation | Approximate result | Interpretation |

COST CONTROL  D2-DEC-07 remains in force: neither $13,300 per capita nor 15.2% of GDP is a baselined final target. The $4.75T central cost position controls until the cost model reconciles population, GDP, time, scope, and price conventions.
