2.3 Failure Modes of the Current System
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Recurring breakdowns such as coverage loss, payment friction, shortages, hospital service closure, and delayed specialty care must be modeled as system behavior rather than anecdotes. Why this structure: Problem statements remain separate from preferred solutions so the comparison does not assume that the framework is the only possible remedy. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes failure modes of the current system explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Define reusable existing-system failure modes, their mechanisms, effects, indicators, and stakeholder links. |

| System entities | All comparator actors and critical infrastructure dependencies. |

| Assumptions | ASM-020–ASM-026, ASM-031–ASM-034. |

| Data / parameters | RISK-BASE-* records, comparator data, event histories, queues, costs, and distributional outcomes. |

| Requirements / performance | Inverse of linked SN; VR-012/013 methods where safety and equity are evaluated. |

| Principal risks | Attributing all adverse events to architecture; ignoring benefits of existing controls; correlated failures; absent recovery behavior. |

| Simulation implication | Failure modes become scenario triggers and state-transition rules; severity, probability, detectability, and mitigations are deferred to Section 10 FMEA. |
The taxonomy below is intentionally pre-FMEA. It names stable failure objects and measurable propagation paths without assigning unsupported probabilities or risk-priority numbers. Later work will add causes, controls, detection, severity, likelihood, recovery, and residual risk.
Table D2-9. Existing-system failure-mode taxonomy

| Risk ID | Failure mode | Mechanism | Effect | Indicators | Needs |

| RISK-BASE-COV-001 | Coverage fragmentation and churn | Eligibility and payer status change with employment, income, age, geography, and program rules | Coverage loss, record/authorization discontinuity, delayed care | uninsured/churn; treatment transfer; medication interruption | SN-02, SN-05 |

| RISK-BASE-AFF-001 | Financial exposure despite coverage | Premiums, deductibles, coinsurance, uncovered benefits, balance bills, and collection practices | Medical debt, delayed or forgone care, household instability | OOP spending; medical debt; problems paying bills | SN-01, SN-12 |

| RISK-BASE-ADM-001 | Administrative fragmentation | Multiple benefit rules, networks, formularies, coding systems, authorization workflows, and claims edits | Provider burden, delay, denial, revenue-cycle cost, patient confusion | admin ratio OI; denial/appeal time; claim cost | SN-06, SN-14, SN-19 |

| RISK-BASE-ACC-001 | Front-door capacity mismatch | Primary and same-day capacity is uneven and disconnected from diagnostic resources | Delayed care, avoidable ED use, untreated chronic need | same-day access OI; low-acuity ED; HPSA indicators | SN-03, SN-18 |

| RISK-BASE-SPEC-001 | Opaque specialist routing | Referral packets, urgency rules, queues, and capacity visibility vary by payer and organization | Delay, duplication, lost referrals, inequitable access | routine/urgent wait OI; referral completion; equity ratio | SN-04, SN-16, SN-18 |

| baseline.market.hospital_consolidation.2024; T-ED-010 | Consolidation and site-payment distortion | Market power, facility ownership, site-based payment, and extraction can reward price or volume rather than service readiness | Higher spending, facility fees, weakened local accountability, closure risk | consolidation; facility fees OI; service continuity | SN-07, SN-11, SN-20 |

| RISK-BASE-RURAL-001 | Rural and tribal access fragility | Low volume, distance, workforce scarcity, capital constraints, and fragmented jurisdiction | Longer travel, service-line loss, inequitable outcomes | travel-time; closures; workforce; tribal compact status | SN-07, SN-18, SN-23, SN-24 |

| RISK-BASE-DRUG-001 | Drug-price and supply-chain failure | Concentrated production, weak redundancy, opaque intermediation, quality problems, and monopoly pricing | Shortage, treatment substitution/delay, fiscal exposure | active/new shortages; price index OI; dual-source rate | SN-08, SN-11, SN-22 |

| RISK-BASE-BEN-001 | Benefit-boundary gaps | Behavioral health, LTC, dental, vision, hearing, EMS, and clinically linked supports are incompletely or inconsistently covered | Untreated need, caregiver burden, institutionalization, avoidable crisis care | unmet need; HPSA population; LTC coverage rule | SN-01, SN-03, SN-05, SN-18 |

| RISK-BASE-DATA-001 | Incomplete interoperability | Data exchange and integration vary across settings and organizations | Duplicate testing, missing medication/history, follow-up failure, migration risk | all-four interoperability; structured record availability | SN-05, SN-15, SN-16 |

| RISK-BASE-CYBER-001 | Concentrated cyber and payment-rail shocks | Critical vendors and providers depend on vulnerable interconnected systems | Care disruption, delayed payment, privacy loss, costly recovery | uptime; continuity drills; cyber event losses | SN-06, SN-13, SN-15 |

| RISK-BASE-GOV-001 | Diffuse accountability and weak repair | Federal, state, payer, provider, contractor, and judicial authorities overlap without a single transparent scorekeeping system | Slow correction, inconsistent rights, capture, executive vulnerability | audit closure; publication; appeal outcomes; trust | SN-13, SN-20, SN-21 |

| RISK-BASE-EQ-001 | Persistent distributional inequity | Coverage, provider supply, language access, disability access, geography, and wealth interact | Unequal access, safety, experience, and outcomes | coverage/access/wait gaps by subgroup and region | SN-18, SN-19, SN-24 |
Selected evidence-to-failure links
RISK-BASE-DATA-001: 70% of nonfederal acute-care hospitals reported engagement in all four interoperability domains in 2023, while routine engagement was lower. Progress and remaining fragmentation must both be represented. [T-ED-012]
RISK-BASE-CYBER-001: GAO reports increased sector cyberattacks and widespread provider/patient-care impacts from the 2024 Change Healthcare ransomware event; architecture-specific propagation and recovery belong in C2 and framework stress scenarios. [T-ED-013]
RISK-BASE-DRUG-001: FDA reported 15 new drug shortages in 2024, while GAO reported 102 active FDA-tracked shortages on July 31, 2024. Stock, flow, duration, product criticality, and substitution cannot be collapsed into one count. [T-ED-014] [T-ED-015]
RISK-BASE-BEN-001: SAMHSA estimated 29.5 million adults with any mental illness received no mental-health treatment in 2024; 6.1 million of that untreated group perceived unmet need. CMS states that Medicare and most insurance do not cover custodial long-term care, subject to program exceptions. [T-ED-016] [T-ED-018]
RISK-BASE-ACC-001 and RISK-BASE-EQ-001: CDC reports approximately 57 million people lived in dental health professional shortage areas in 2024, with about 67% of shortage areas in rural communities. [T-ED-017]
Section 2 CONCLUSION  The comparator is an evolving, heterogeneous system with real strengths and identifiable structural failure modes. D2 establishes a sourced macro/coverage/debt/workforce/interoperability/supply baseline and preserves major access, administrative, quality, equity, and incidence measures as calibration gaps rather than invented numbers.
3. Assumptions
PART DECISION QUESTION  What is inside the framework and the comparison, what premises control the design, how are the four cost quantities interpreted, and what evaluation rules prevent the simulation from manufacturing success?
3.1 Scope Boundaries
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Without explicit boundaries, the framework could be credited with benefits it does not produce or charged with solving problems outside its authority. Why this structure: Assumptions are controlled objects so uncertainty can be varied, challenged, and traced instead of becoming an invisible premise. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes scope boundaries explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Define population, benefit, institutional, financial, geographic, temporal, and comparison boundaries. |

| System entities | Eligible residents; NHA and residual private plans; federal/state/regional/tribal entities; providers/facilities; employers; households; legacy payers; public-health and social-service interfaces. |

| Assumptions | ASM-003–ASM-006, ASM-014, ASM-017–ASM-020, ASM-023, ASM-028–ASM-029. |

| Data / parameters | CP-TOT, CP-POP, CP-FIN; benefit classes; geography/jurisdiction; payer and cost ledgers. |

| Requirements / performance | SR-COV; SR-LTC/BH/DVH/EMS; SR-ARCH; KPP-A/C/E; TPP-EMP/REG/TRIB. |

| Principal risks | Scope creep; exclusion error; double payment; cost shifting; state/tribal conflict; inconsistent population denominators. |

| Simulation implication | Scope fields are required dimensions in every cost, utilization, coverage, and outcome record. |
Scope is a computable boundary, not a prose disclaimer. Every service, person, payment, institution, and outcome included in a cost or performance result must carry a boundary classification. When a service moves from excluded or conditional to core coverage, the change is versioned and its cost, capacity, legal, and equity effects are re-evaluated.
Table D2-10. Controlled scope matrix

| Boundary | In scope | Conditional / residual | Out of core scope |

| Population | Eligible U.S. residents under the final statutory definition; provisional coverage for unresolved status | Territories, cross-border care, nonresident emergency care, and substitute coverage require rules | No silent exclusion from denominators; final eligibility definition remains OI-001/OI-010 adjacent |

| Core clinical benefit | Covered medically necessary prevention, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, essential drugs, and defined devices/supports | Novel, low-value, preference-sensitive, experimental, or nonstandard care under transparent review | Purely cosmetic/luxury services unless medically necessary under controlled criteria |

| Expanded benefit | Defined LTC, behavioral health, dental, vision, hearing, EMS, public health, and linked supports | Capacity- and phase-gated services; setting and intensity rules | General social policy without a documented clinical nexus |

| Private roles | Certified fixed-fee administrative services and permitted supplemental/substitute roles | Noncovered benefits and statutory exceptions with anti-duplication controls | Commercial duplication of the core public risk pool or PBM control of the core pharmacy benefit |

| Public finance | Redirected public spending, dedicated receipts, employer contributions, and certified public outlays | Reserve contributions/draws, residual private spending, patient noncovered spending | Unrelated government programs and general social expenditures |

| Institutional | DNHA and all controlled authorities; participating public/private providers and vendors | State/compact administration, tribal agreements, certified contractors, legacy wind-down | Institutions with no framework function except as external environment |

| Geography | National, region, state, rural/frontier, urban, tribal jurisdiction, and territories as defined | Cross-region referral, telehealth, border services, direct federal fallback | Foreign systems except supply, migration, pricing, or care interfaces explicitly modeled |

| Time | 2024 baseline; 10–12-year transition; maturity; extended risk horizon | Year-15 NHTCA sunset and 2034/2038 external forecast anchors | Timeless equilibrium without transition and cohort effects |
Cost-view boundary

| View | Included | Excluded from that view | Primary parameter |

| Total-system | Public + residual private + patient-paid health spending within scope | Reserve fund balance as a stock; nonhealth general social spending | CP-TOT-001 |

| Public budget | Federal and applicable state/local health outlays and transfers | Residual private premiums/spending; household noncovered spending | CP-TOT-004 / CP-FIN |

| Household | Taxes/contributions borne, premiums, point-of-care and noncovered spending, debt effects | Transfers not economically incident on households | CP-TOT-006 / CP-FIN-017 |

| Employer | Contributions, administration, wage pass-through, transition obligations | Unrelated compensation and business costs | CP-FIN-004/018/019 |

| Transition | Time-limited build, migration, continuity, stabilization, and wind-down | Recurring mature operations; reserve stock | CP-TOT-007 / CP-TR |

| Reserve | Opening balance, contribution, earnings, draw, transfer, closing balance | Consumption cost unless a contribution is an outlay in the chosen fiscal view | CP-FIN-011–016 |
BOUNDARY OPEN ITEMS  The computational categories are controlled for D2, but the final eligible-population definition, detailed covered-benefit rule, substitute-plan standard, and clinically linked social-support test remain open under OI-001, OI-005, and OI-010.
3.2 Core Design Assumptions
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: The design depends on behavioral, legal, capacity, fiscal, and technological propositions that must remain visible instead of being embedded invisibly in prose or code. Why this structure: Assumptions are controlled objects so uncertainty can be varied, challenged, and traced instead of becoming an invisible premise. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes core design assumptions explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Publish the complete Sections 1–3 assumption register and distinguish baselined framework premises from proposed model assumptions and open issues. |

| System entities | All framework elements, comparator actors, data authorities, and simulation modules. |

| Assumptions | ASM-001–ASM-035. |

| Data / parameters | Source authority, status, linked objects, parameter use, sensitivity, and closure criteria for each assumption. |

| Requirements / performance | Assumptions link to applicable SN, PR/SR/VR, KPP/TPP, CP, ARCH, RISK, and SCN records. |

| Principal risks | Hidden premises; contradictory assumptions; unsupported precision; failure to update downstream objects after revision. |

| Simulation implication | Every assumption becomes a versioned switch, prior, constraint, or interpretation rule; uncertainty and alternatives remain explicit. |
An assumption is not an external fact and not an achieved outcome. Baselined assumptions control the present design. Proposed assumptions are needed to build the model but remain subject to evidence and review. Open assumptions identify a value or definition that the document cannot responsibly resolve at this stage.
Source-controlled design assumptions
Table D2-11. Source-controlled design assumptions

| ID | Name | Status / class | Controlled statement | Links | Simulation treatment |

| ASM-001 | R&D delinkage | Baselined / FA | Drug prices should not be the primary mechanism for recovering biomedical R&D cost. | ARCH-NBIA; CP-RD; SN-22 | Compare monopoly-price recovery with public R&D funding; vary innovation productivity and licensing terms. |

| ASM-002 | Public innovation funding | Baselined / FA | A separate public biomedical innovation system funds high-priority drug and technology development. | ARCH-NBIA; TPP-13.1 | Model annual portfolio funding, probability of success, time to adoption, and public-interest license conditions. |

| ASM-003 | Public default coverage | Baselined / FA | Public default coverage is the primary core-coverage model. | SN-02; SR-COV; ARCH-NEEA; ARCH-NCCA | Enrollment is a state transition; residual noncoverage is an error/exception outcome, not the design default. |

| ASM-004 | Residual private roles | Baselined with OI-005 | Private plans may exist only in certified supplemental, substitute, or fixed-fee administrative roles. | ARCH-PPCO; CP-TOT-005 | Separate benefit, risk, premium, and duplication ledgers; run alternative boundary scenarios until certification rules close. |

| ASM-005 | PBM displacement | Baselined / FA | PBMs are removed from the core public pharmacy benefit. | ARCH-PCU/NDPA; TPP-3.4 | Route core claims through the public utility; retain explicit legacy wind-down and residual private-plan cases. |

| ASM-006 | Point-of-care price | Baselined / FA | Covered medically necessary care has zero or near-zero consumer price at the point of care. | SN-01; KPP-A3/A5 | Patient price approaches zero, but utilization, capacity, total cost, and noncovered spending remain endogenous. |

| ASM-007 | Capacity-before-price gate | Baselined / FA | Capacity expansion precedes broad national removal of cost sharing. | PR-SCH-011; KPP-B7 | Cost-sharing state change is disabled until the 80% unit-coverage gate and applicable safety gates pass. |

| ASM-008 | Specialist constraint | Baselined / FA | Specialist capacity is a binding constraint and cannot be treated as infinitely elastic. | SN-04; RISK-SPEC-001 | Use specialty-region queues, service times, protected capacity, e-consult substitution, and workforce lags. |

| ASM-009 | Human-accountable AI | Baselined / FA | AI may assist but may not finally decide specified high-stakes denials, non-referrals, non-escalations, LTC reductions, benefit terminations, or diagnoses. | SN-17; TPP-11.5 | High-stakes decisions require human-review states, override logs, error/equity monitoring, and suspension scenarios. |

| ASM-010 | Transition as primary risk | Baselined / FA | Transition failure is a primary system risk, not a secondary administrative issue. | Layer 3; RISK-DATA-001 | Continuity failure, legacy payer behavior, data migration, and cash-flow shocks are modeled explicitly. |

| ASM-011 | Hospital continuity constraint | Baselined / FA | Hospital savings are constrained by essential-service continuity, safe staffing, and rural readiness. | SN-07; TPP-5.4/5.5 | Budget reductions cannot be counted as savings when they violate service or staffing constraints. |

| ASM-012 | Federated information mesh | Baselined / FA | The Information Mesh is federated public infrastructure rather than a single uncontrolled database. | ARCH-NHRA; SN-15 | Model distributed nodes, common identity/locator services, access controls, latency, downtime, and recovery. |

| ASM-013 | Durable but repairable | Baselined / FA | The system must resist sabotage while remaining correctable through transparent, evidence-based, legally bounded repair. | Layer 5; SN-13/SN-21 | Represent repair authority, delay, sunset, rollback, court constraints, and anti-impoundment failures. |

| ASM-014 | Clinically linked social supports | Baselined with OI-010 | Social supports enter the core framework only when clinically linked; general housing, income, and food policy remain outside scope absent medical linkage. | Scope boundary; CP-SOC | Apply eligibility and causal-link rules; prevent general social-program costs from entering CP-TOT-001 without a controlled scope change. |

| ASM-015 | Framework-number status | Baselined / FA | Framework-specific quantitative values remain model assumptions unless independently sourced. | All framework cost and target records | The engine retains source_class and must never convert an FA or TG into ED through repetition. |

ASSUMPTION CHANGE RULE  Changing an ASM object requires impact review of every linked requirement, parameter, architecture element, risk, scenario, equation, and result. An assumption may be rejected or superseded, but its ID is not recycled.
3.3 Final Framework Cost Assumptions
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: The cost numbers are policy assumptions, not observed outcomes; their price year, scope, range, and transition treatment must be stated before they are repeated. Why this structure: Assumptions are controlled objects so uncertainty can be varied, challenged, and traced instead of becoming an invisible premise. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes final framework cost assumptions explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.

| Quantity | Controlled value | Class | Model role |

MASTER COST  C_total_system(t) = Σ C_operating_categories(t) + C_transition_net(t) − C_offsets(t) + C_residual_private(t) + C_patient_paid(t)
The detailed category expansion remains controlled by the Source Package. Public outlay, reserve stock, and financing receipts are separate views and must reconcile without being substituted for total-system cost.
TRANSITION CONTROL  Σ_t C_transition_incremental(t) ∈ [$1.2T, $2.0T],  t ∈ transition years
Each transition event has one event ID, subledger, phase, owner, and annual amount. If a capability becomes recurring, the enduring amount transfers to operating cost and leaves the transition ledger.
NET SAVINGS  CP-TOT-008(t) = C_existing_comparator(t) − C_framework_total_system(t)
Net savings is calculated only after both systems are aligned on population, price year, service boundary, geography, and time. Gross additions and gross offsets remain visible.

3.4 Evaluation Assumptions
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: A comparison can be biased by its time horizon, comparator, discounting, or treatment of uncertainty unless the evaluation rules are fixed in advance. Why this structure: Assumptions are controlled objects so uncertainty can be varied, challenged, and traced instead of becoming an invisible premise. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes evaluation assumptions explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Define comparator symmetry, perspectives, horizons, uncertainty, validation, and decision rules for evaluation. |

| System entities | Framework and comparator modules; NHASB; CHAO; NHAC; independent verifiers; data authorities; simulation builders. |

| Assumptions | ASM-020, ASM-023–ASM-034. |

| Data / parameters | Inputs, state variables, outputs, evidence, distributions, scenario controls, validation sets, and version metadata. |

| Requirements / performance | VR-001–VR-015; every KPP/TPP; phase gates and requirement pass/fail rules. |

| Principal risks | Asymmetric assumptions; policy-target clipping; selective time horizons; missing distributional effects; double counting; nonreproducible results. |

| Simulation implication | The engine must report mechanisms, uncertainty, failures, and limitations for both systems under aligned scenarios. |
Table D2-17. Evaluation design rules

| Rule | Controlled convention | Simulation implementation |

| Comparator symmetry | Align population, economy, price year, geography, service boundary, and shocks. | Shared exogenous inputs; architecture-specific response functions |

| Static + dynamic | Report 2024 state and annual transition/counterfactual trajectories. | C0, C1, C2 and F0/F1/F2 scenario families |

| Multiple perspectives | Total-system, federal, state/local, employer, household, provider, and distributional views. | Separate ledgers and transfer reconciliation |

| No forced compliance | Targets and requirements are evaluated against outputs. | Pass/Fail/Indeterminate/NA; no clipping to threshold |

| Causal cost discipline | Every offset has pathway, lag, attribution, and uncertainty. | Event and cost IDs; duplicate-savings detection |

| Capacity realism | Queues, lead times, workforce, facilities, and supply constrain service. | Stock-flow and discrete-event components |

| Equity | Report prespecified geography and population strata with privacy rules. | Gap/ratio outputs, uncertainty, suppression metadata |

| Uncertainty | Use ranges/distributions, correlations, structural alternatives, and threshold analysis. | Monte Carlo or other documented sampling plus deterministic stress cases |

| Validation | Separate calibration and validation evidence where feasible. | Dataset role, holdout status, fit and predictive checks |

| Reproducibility | Version data, code, formulas, parameters, random seeds, and overrides. | Immutable run manifest and output provenance |

| Independent verification | Gate-relevant and safety measures require independent evidence. | Verifier role and evidence artifact in result record |

| Limitations | Unresolved questions remain visible and bound interpretation. | OI list in every report; no hidden default completion |
Primary evaluation outputs for Sections 1–3

| Output family | Required measures | Comparison |

| Coverage/financial protection | coverage continuity, uninsured, patient billing, OOP, debt, bankruptcy proxy | level, change, subgroup gap, transition failure |

| Access/capacity | front-door wait, same-day resolution, travel, queues, specialist waits, urgent completion | distribution and tail risk, not mean only |

| Quality/safety | avoidable use, readmission, prevention, chronic control, diagnostic/follow-up events | risk-adjusted and equity-stratified |

| Workforce/provider | staff stock, vacancies, workload, compensation, payment timeliness, administrative time | occupation, specialty, setting, region |

| Cost/fiscal | total-system, public outlay, payer/household/employer burden, revenue, reserves, transition | annual and cumulative, real 2024 dollars |

| Rights/legitimacy | explanation, appeal, correction, privacy, trust, publication, human review | timeliness, completion, reversals, disparities |

| Resilience | downtime, continuity, shortage, fiscal/cyber/legal shock, recovery time | shared shock with architecture-specific propagation |
Section 3 CONCLUSION  D2 establishes computable scope categories, expands the assumption register to ASM-001–ASM-035, preserves the four final cost quantities as framework assumptions, and blocks target-as-outcome behavior. The central cost position remains controlling, while per-capita and GDP targets remain open pending denominator and maturity-year reconciliation.
4. Views
4.1 Stakeholder View
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Patients, clinicians, hospitals, workers, governments, and taxpayers experience different benefits and burdens, so no single institutional viewpoint is sufficient. Why this structure: Each view isolates one stakeholder concern while cross-references preserve the interfaces that make the system operate as a whole. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes stakeholder view explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Allocate each top-level stakeholder need to an affected stakeholder, service owner, right, information requirement, performance measure, risk, and simulation output. |

| System entities | Patients; households; providers; facilities; workforce; employers; states/regions; tribal nations; sponsors; oversight bodies; innovators; public. |

| Assumptions | ASM-003–ASM-014, ASM-018, ASM-021–ASM-034. |

| Data / parameters | SN-01–SN-25; linked KPP/TPP; event, denominator, equity, rights, and evidence fields. |

| Requirements / performance | All need-linked PR/SR/VR; ARCH owner; IF dependence; risk and scenario links. |

| Principal risks | Stakeholder collapse; proxy measures; inaccessible process; rights without remedy; conflicting objectives; hidden distributional burden. |

| Simulation implication | Needs become objective/constraint records; stakeholder and equity strata are mandatory dimensions of outputs. |
The stakeholder view is solution-neutral at the SN level and solution-allocating below it. The owner column identifies the accountable service owner, not the only contributing organization. NHAC, NHASB, CHAO, and the Article I court retain independent roles even when an operating office owns delivery.

Stakeholder conflict rules
Clinical safety and enforceable rights are constraints, not weights that may be traded away for average cost or throughput.
When stakeholder objectives conflict, the engine records the conflict and applicable authority; it does not silently collapse all objectives into one utility score.
National results are reported with regional and protected/vulnerable-group distributions. A favorable mean cannot erase a failed safety or equity gate.
Employer, state, vendor, or provider convenience cannot terminate public default coverage or bar an appeal.
Tribal sovereignty and federal trust responsibilities are represented directly, not as a state-government subgroup.
SECTION 4.1 RESULT  All 25 top-level needs now have an accountable service owner, explicit right/remedy concept, derived service content, measure, and simulation treatment. This is a traceability allocation, not proof that any target is achieved.
4.2 Requirements View
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: A policy aspiration cannot guide procurement, law, or verification until it is converted into allocated, testable obligations. Why this structure: Each view isolates one stakeholder concern while cross-references preserve the interfaces that make the system operate as a whole. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes requirements view explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Normalize and allocate every source-controlled PR and SR while defining how VR requirements constrain verification. |

| System entities | Requirement owners; independent verifiers; stakeholders; architecture elements; data and interface authorities; phase-gate authorities. |

| Assumptions | ASM-015, ASM-017–ASM-020, ASM-023–ASM-035. |

| Data / parameters | 45 PR; 183 SR; 30 VR; status, trace, method, owner, verifier, phase, evidence, risk, and simulation link fields. |

| Requirements / performance | SN-01–SN-25; all PR/SR/VR; linked KPP/TPP; ARCH and IF allocations. |

| Principal risks | Conflicting target; orphan requirement; owner/verifier collision; false closure; unverifiable shall; missing denominator or authority. |

| Simulation implication | Each requirement becomes a versioned rule with Pass/Fail/Indeterminate/Not Applicable result and evidence provenance. |
NORMAL FORM  ID + normative statement + source trace + accountable owner + independent verifier/method + status. Later deliverables add data dictionary, acceptance threshold, phase, evidence artifact, risk, and scenario links without changing the requirement ID.

4.3 Organizational Architecture View
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Eighty-two institutional elements are incomprehensible as a flat catalog; readers need to see which elements operate, oversee, pay, adjudicate, transition, or adapt the system. Why this structure: Each view isolates one stakeholder concern while cross-references preserve the interfaces that make the system operate as a whole. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes organizational architecture view explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Define organizational topology, authority boundaries, separation of powers, and escalation paths for the framework. |

| System entities | Congress; Treasury/IRS/THDO; DNHA and administrations; NHAC; NHASB; CHAO; Article I court; RHA; state/regional/tribal partners. |

| Assumptions | ASM-009–ASM-013, ASM-018, ASM-023–ASM-024, ASM-029–ASM-034. |

| Data / parameters | ARCH catalog; decision records; authority state; vacancies; conflicts; delegation; compact and fallback status. |

| Requirements / performance | SR-ARCH-001–015; SR-LAW; SR-RGT; SR-ADP; VR-001/003/019/021/022/025. |

| Principal risks | Concentrated authority; orphan decision; owner/verifier collision; vacancy paralysis; forum delay; regional ambiguity; capture. |

| Simulation implication | Organizations are agents with bounded actions, decision rights, dependencies, vacancy state, and fallback behaviors. |
The architecture separates operation, rights protection, scorekeeping/adaptation, legislative audit, fiscal execution, regional delivery, and judicial remedy. Coordination is required; consolidation of these roles into one chain of command is prohibited because it would allow the same body to create a rule, operate it, grade it, and deny a remedy.

4.4 Governing Agency Breakdown
WHY NINE INSTITUTIONS  The design does not create nine bodies merely to distribute work. It separates five powers that should not be collapsed: operating care and coverage; moving public money; independently protecting rights and safety; measuring and repairing system performance; and issuing enforceable remedies. Transition command and biomedical innovation are also separated because their time horizons and incentives differ from ordinary operations.
Figure 4.4-1. DNHA major compositional hierarchy

Figure 4.4-2. NHAC major compositional hierarchy

Figure 4.4-3. NHTCA major compositional hierarchy

Figure 4.4-4. NBIA compositional hierarchy

4.4.1 Department of National Health Assurance (ARCH-DNHA)
What it does. DNHA is the operating department. It turns statutory coverage into enrollment, benefit rules, claims operations, medicine and device programs, workforce policy, records infrastructure, hospital stewardship, and regional care delivery.
Why this structure. It is broad because care delivery, payment rules, workforce, medicines, and information constrain one another. It is not permitted to certify its own success, control final judicial remedies, or use operational convenience to erase statutory rights.
How it interacts. THDO pays DNHA-authorized obligations; NHAC oversees rights and safety; NHTCA protects conversion; NHASB verifies results and controls repair; Regional Health Administrators execute capacity plans.
4.4.2 National Health Accountability Commission (ARCH-NHAC)
What it does. NHAC is the independent public-protection institution. It receives complaints, protects privacy and patient rights, investigates safety and extraction, grants defined provisional relief, audits affected cases, and publishes performance information.
Why this structure. It is separate from DNHA so the operator is not the final investigator or reviewer of its own conduct. NHAC cannot appropriate funds, operate coverage, or replace an Article I court judgment.
How it interacts. It receives records from DNHA and THDO, refers systemic issues to NHASB and CHAO, supports appeals, and can seek enforceable relief in the Article I Court.
4.4.3 National Biomedical Innovation Agency (ARCH-NBIA)
What it does. NBIA finances discovery, translation, trials, comparative effectiveness, and secure research while attaching affordability and access conditions to public funding.
Why this structure. It is separate from purchasing and formulary operations so scientific investment is not reduced to a short-term procurement decision and purchasing leverage is not confused with research merit.
How it interacts. NBIA works with the PMC and drug-purchasing authority on unmet needs, with the licensing office on public rights, with CEVI on comparative evidence, and with NHASB on long-run performance.
4.4.4 Treasury Health Disbursement Office (ARCH-THDO)
What it does. THDO is the protected payment executor. It sends authorized claims, pharmacy payments, hospital budgets, workforce payments, and other statutory health obligations through a mandatory Treasury rail.
Why this structure. It is placed in Treasury and separated from coverage operations to reduce the risk that an operating agency or executive official can delay lawful payment as leverage over patients or providers.
How it interacts. DNHA and authorized budget bodies create validated obligations; NHETF and the assurance trust provide funds; THDO returns immutable payment status to providers, NHAC, CHAO, and the Article I Court.
4.4.5 National Health Equalization Trust Fund (ARCH-NHETF)
What it does. NHETF is the shock absorber. It contains operating stabilization resources, a transition and emergency reserve, and a permanent health endowment.
Why this structure. A separate trust prevents ordinary annual operating pressure from consuming all reserves and makes drawdown, replenishment, and investment rules visible to Congress and the public.
How it interacts. The financing actuary certifies adequacy, NHASB tests triggers, Treasury holds assets, THDO disburses authorized amounts, and CHAO reports interference or improper diversion.
4.4.6 National Health Transition and Continuity Authority (ARCH-NHTCA)
What it does. NHTCA is a temporary but powerful conversion command responsible for ensuring that active care, medications, provider cash flow, hospitals, records, workers, employers, and intergovernmental compacts survive the transition.
Why this structure. Transition risk is concentrated and time-dependent, so it requires one cross-domain authority rather than leaving every new permanent agency to protect only its own implementation schedule.
How it interacts. It coordinates with every permanent institution, operates phase-gate evidence with NHASB, and sunsets or transfers functions after defined stabilization evidence is achieved.
4.4.7 National Health Adaptation and Scorekeeping Board (ARCH-NHASB)
What it does. NHASB maintains independent scorekeeping, the formula registry, scheduled and triggered reviews, red-team exercises, sunset decisions, regional-waiver evaluation, and controlled repair proposals.
Why this structure. It is separate from DNHA and NHTCA so agencies cannot declare their own targets met or quietly change formulas to hide failure. It may control configuration and recommend repair but cannot silently reduce statutory rights.
How it interacts. It consumes operational and fiscal data, certifies gate evidence, reports to Congress and the public, sends rights issues to NHAC, and activates legal or fiscal fallbacks through preauthorized rules.
4.4.8 Congressional Health Accountability Office (ARCH-CHAO)
What it does. CHAO is Congress's dedicated visibility and continuity institution. It monitors impoundment, vacancies, interference, reporting failures, payment obstruction, and executive nonperformance.
Why this structure. Ordinary executive-branch oversight is insufficient when the alleged failure is executive refusal itself; an Article I office preserves evidence and reporting outside the operating chain.
How it interacts. CHAO receives protected feeds from THDO, NHETF, NHASB, and NHAC; reports to Congress; and may support expedited Article I court action or statutory fallback activation.
4.4.9 Article I Health Claims and Appeals Court (ARCH-A1-HCAC)
What it does. The Article I Court supplies expedited, enforceable remedies for patient entitlement, provider payment, anti-impoundment, and urgent continuity disputes.
Why this structure. Administrative review alone leaves final authority inside the executive branch. A specialized court provides independent fact finding, uniform remedies, and deadlines suited to care and payment harms that cannot wait for ordinary litigation.
How it interacts. It receives exhausted or emergency claims, can review NHAC and administrative records, directs lawful payment or relief, and remains institutionally separate from DNHA, THDO, and NHASB.
4.4.10 Separation-of-powers and interface summary
Table 4.4-1. Institutional decision boundaries

| Decision | Primary authority | Independent check | What is deliberately separated |

| Coverage and operating rule | DNHA / delegated authority | NHAC, NHASB, and court review | Rulemaking is separated from final rights enforcement and performance certification. |

| Validated public payment | THDO execution | CHAO and Article I remedies | Payment execution is separated from benefit adjudication and ordinary executive discretion. |

| Reserve trigger | NHETF under certified formula | HFASB, NHASB, and Congress | Reserve custody is separated from operating demand and formula certification. |

| Transition expansion | NHTCA under phase authority | NHASB gate verification and NHAC continuity review | Schedule control is separated from independent readiness evidence. |

| Rights or safety remedy | NHAC provisional/administrative action | Article I Court | The operator cannot be the final reviewer of its own action. |

| System repair | NHASB controlled process | Congress, NHAC, and judicial review | Repair cannot silently amend entitlement or extinguish accrued rights. |
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: The nine top-level institutions divide powers that are currently fragmented or conflicted; the separation only makes sense if each body's purpose, boundaries, and interactions are explained. Why this structure: Each view isolates one stakeholder concern while cross-references preserve the interfaces that make the system operate as a whole. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes governing agency breakdown explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Provide a complete machine-addressable catalog of the source-controlled architecture elements and their accountable roles. |

| System entities | All ARCH elements in the Source Package; nonfederal partners and regulated actors as external participants. |

The 82 entries below are the explicit Architecture Catalog in the authoritative Source Package. Mentions of SR-ARCH-001–015 are requirements and are not additional agencies. External actors such as providers, pharmacies, hospitals, employers, states, and tribal nations participate through contracts, compacts, rights, and interfaces rather than being recoded as federal ARCH elements.
Agency lifecycle and continuity rules
Permanent bodies require statutory authority, funding continuity, succession, records custody, and vacancy fallback.
ARCH-NHTCA and transition suboffices are time-limited; closure requires transfer of unresolved cases, records, liabilities, and continuing functions.
A parent administration may coordinate a subauthority but may not absorb an independent oversight, scorekeeping, legislative-audit, or judicial function.
Delegation must identify delegator, delegate, scope, start/expiration, review, and revocation; unrecorded delegation has no simulation authority.
Abolition, merger, or renaming requires an impact review across all linked PR/SR/VR, IF, risks, phases, formulas, and remedies.

4.5 Functional Architecture View
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: An organization chart does not show how enrollment becomes care, how care becomes payment, or how a denial becomes a remedy; end-to-end functions must cross institutional boundaries. Why this structure: Each view isolates one stakeholder concern while cross-references preserve the interfaces that make the system operate as a whole. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes functional architecture view explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Describe the transformations the system performs independently of any single organization chart. |

| System entities | All operating, fiscal, rights, information, transition, and adaptation authorities; external service actors. |

| Assumptions | ASM-003–ASM-014, ASM-017–ASM-035. |

| Data / parameters | Inputs, outputs, events, queues, state variables, resources, formulas, owners, IF dependencies, failure/recovery states. |

| Requirements / performance | All SR families; PR-SCH/PR-TRN; VR-001–030; KPP/TPP; IF-001–032. |

| Principal risks | Function without owner; interface without function; feedback delay; stale state; unclosed episode; unsafe optimization; double counting. |

| Simulation implication | Functional rows become simulation modules, event handlers, state transitions, resources, queues, and result producers. |
Functional authority follows the business obligation, not data custody. For example, NHRA may carry a referral record, but NSAA owns specialty routing; THDO moves payment, but NCCA owns adjudication; NHASB verifies a phase gate, but the implementing authority owns corrective action.
Table D3-11. Functional decomposition and simulation allocation

| Function | Requirement family | Transformation | Accountable owner | State / output | Interfaces |

| Coverage and eligibility | SR-COV | identify resident; establish/provision coverage; maintain continuity; certify residual private role | ARCH-NEEA | coverage_state; eligibility_event; termination_reason | IF-001–IF-002 |

| Claims and payment | SR-PAY | validate covered service; adjudicate obligation; disburse; reconcile; remedy | ARCH-NCCA | claim_state; obligation; disbursement_state | IF-003–IF-004 |

| Medicines and supply | SR-DRUG | maintain formulary; purchase; adjudicate pharmacy claim; monitor shortage; manufacture backup | ARCH-AMDDT | drug_access_class; inventory; shortage_state | IF-005–IF-006 |

| Hospital stewardship | SR-HOSP | certify charter; set global budget; protect service lines; fund capital/readiness; audit variance | ARCH-NHSA | budget_state; service_line_state; readiness | IF-013–IF-014 |

| Front-door access | SR-ACC | route request; select unit/channel; diagnose/treat; escalate; close follow-up | ARCH-OCDTI | care_state; acuity; unit_type; follow_up_state | IF-007; IF-011 |

| Specialty routing | SR-SPEC | complete workup; classify urgency; consult; reserve slot; complete referral; return plan | ARCH-NSAA | routing_level; urgency_class; queue_position | IF-008–IF-010 |

| Expanded benefits | SR-LTC/BH/DVH/EMS | assess need; authorize covered pathway; coordinate service and transport; reassess | ARCH-ACDRH | benefit_pathway; assessment_state; capacity | IF-011–IF-012 |

| Records and interoperability | SR-DATA | resolve identity; locate/retrieve records; exchange; correct; audit; fail over | ARCH-AHIRC | record_locator; access_event; correction_state | IF-016–IF-019 |

| AI accountability | SR-AI | register; classify; validate; assist; capture human review; monitor; suspend | ARCH-AICIO | model_version; use_class; review_state | IF-020 |

| Rights and appeals | SR-RGT | explain; notify; accept complaint/appeal; grant interim relief; decide; execute remedy | ARCH-NHAC | decision_record; appeal_state; remedy_state | IF-021–IF-022; IF-031 |

| Equity | SR-EQ | stratify; detect gap; investigate; order correction; monitor closure | ARCH-NOPRSL | equity_stratum; gap; correction_state | IF-023; IF-032 |

| Fiscal/legal continuity | SR-LAW | certify obligation; protect disbursement; monitor interference; invoke fallback; enforce | ARCH-CHAO | authority_state; reserve_state; legal_shock | IF-024–IF-025 |

| Innovation | SR-INN | prioritize unmet need; fund; license; translate; evaluate; assure access | ARCH-NBIA | program_state; milestone; license_state | IF-029–IF-030 |

| Adaptation and repair | SR-ADP | score; detect drift/failure; register formula; review; repair/sunset; verify | ARCH-NHASB | formula_version; change_tier; sunset_state | IF-027–IF-028; IF-032 |

| Transition continuity | PR-TRN / SR-IF | inventory legacy state; migrate; bridge; reconcile; stabilize; wind down | ARCH-NHTCA | migration_state; bridge_state; continuity_event | IF-026–IF-028 |
End-to-end functional threads

| Thread | Entry | Controlled sequence | Exit / closure | Recovery |

| Coverage-to-payment | resident/service event | identity → coverage → benefit/claim → obligation → THDO settlement → reconciliation | paid, explained denial, or appeal/remedy | provisional coverage/payment; failover rail |

| Front door-to-specialist | care request | triage → Type A–D/primary care → workup → urgency → consult/slot → completion → return plan | closed-loop follow-up owner | red-flag escalation; protected slot; EMS |

| Hospital budget | certified regional need | charter → operating/readiness/capital build → fiscal certification → disbursement → variance/service monitoring | year close and next budget | stabilization corridor; corrective plan |

| Rights/remedy | decision, delay, safety event, complaint | complete record → notice → reconsideration/rights review → provisional relief → Article I remedy | executed remedy and learning event | stay, manual case, escalation |

| Transition | legacy person/provider/record/payment | inventory → map → migrate → bridge → reconcile → stabilize → wind down | continuity confirmed; liability assigned | rollback, dual run, cash-flow/medication guarantee |

| Adaptation | metric drift, failure, legal/technical shock | detect → score → classify change → test → notice/review → deploy → monitor/sunset | verified repair or rollback | emergency correction with expiration |
FUNCTIONAL CLOSURE  request → accountable disposition → recorded owner → verified closure
A throughput event is not complete merely because it leaves one agency queue. Closure is end-to-end and includes patient/provider notice, follow-up, payment/remedy where applicable, and evidence provenance.
4.6 Care-Delivery View
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Public coverage is useful only if people can reach appropriate care through a safe front door, specialty route, hospital pathway, and continuity mechanism. Why this structure: Each view isolates one stakeholder concern while cross-references preserve the interfaces that make the system operate as a whole. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes care-delivery view explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Specify patient/provider journeys, Type A–D responsibilities, specialist routing states, hospital payment boundaries, and continuity fallbacks. |

| System entities | Patients; primary care; Type A–D units; NSAA; specialists; EMS; hospitals; pharmacies; RHAs; NHAC; NHTCA. |

| Assumptions | ASM-006–ASM-011, ASM-021–ASM-026, ASM-030–ASM-034. |

| Data / parameters | request, acuity, unit type, capability, referral packet, urgency, capacity ledger, protected slot, service line, continuity event. |

| Requirements / performance | SR-ACC, SR-SPEC, SR-HOSP, SR-LTC/BH/DVH/EMS, SR-RGT/EQ; KPP-B; TPP-5/6/9; VR-012–018. |

| Principal risks | Under-referral; queue gaming; fragmented follow-up; unit scope creep; primary-care displacement; rural transfer failure; hospital destabilization. |

| Simulation implication | Discrete-event care states, resource pools, routing logic, wait distributions, failure/recovery events, and subgroup outcomes. |
The diagnostic-treatment network supplements rather than replaces relationship-based primary care. It absorbs protocol-suitable measurable work while preserving primary care for complexity, continuity, frailty, disability, multimorbidity, family context, and goals of care. Capacity is explicit: no access target assumes infinitely elastic clinicians, diagnostics, transport, or hospital services.
Table D3-12. Four-unit diagnostic-treatment network responsibility matrix

| Unit | Role / setting | Minimum service envelope | Mandatory escalation | Simulation fields |

| Type A Micro-Unit | Very low complexity, distributed or mobile | vitals; basic point-of-care tests; vaccines; refills; screening; teleclinician support | red flag, unresolved abnormal result, complexity outside protocol | unit_type=A; capability_set; escalation_event |

| Type B Standard Neighborhood Unit | Default neighborhood diagnostic-treatment access | ECG; basic labs/X-ray; common procedures; splinting; nebulizer; limited ultrasound; common acute care; chronic measurement | red flag; failed protocol; diagnostic uncertainty; specialty/hospital need | unit_type=B; diagnostic_bundle; disposition |

| Type C Rural Enhanced Unit | Rural/frontier enhanced access and resilience | Type B plus tele-specialty; observation; EMS coordination; POCUS; limited IV; maternal/pediatric triage; mobile/weather resilience | unstable patient; unavailable local capability; time-sensitive disease | unit_type=C; travel_time; weather_state; transfer_state |

| Type D Urban/Public Health Unit | High-volume urban and public-health access | respiratory surge; vaccines; STI/reproductive services; behavioral/addiction linkage; wound care; climate/public-health response | higher-acuity clinical need; public-health escalation; specialty/hospital need | unit_type=D; surge_state; outreach_event |

| 1 | Protocol management | standardized plan with automated follow-up | protocol; checkpoint; exception |

| 3 | Tele-specialist | synchronous remote specialist encounter | appointment; completion; disposition |

| T-ED-001 | Expedited | 1–2 weeks |

Structured referral packet and capacity ledger

| Object | Required fields | Accountable owner | Failure response |

| Referral packet | problem representation; clinical question; red-flag screen; tests; treatments; medications; images/labs; constraints; urgency; follow-up owner | referring team; NSAA validates | return for completion only if safe; never delay a red-flag route |

| Specialty capacity ledger | specialty; region; modality; slot class; opening; reservation; queue; downtime | NSAA / RHA | protect urgent capacity; cross-region/tele route; workforce/capacity action |

| Protected-slot plan | urgent; e-consult; tele; new patient; complex follow-up; procedure planning | NSAA / specialty service | variance investigation and corrective allocation |

| Closure record | response; appointment/completion; plan; results; patient notice; follow-up owner | specialist and referring team | escalate overdue closure and retain shared accountability |
Hospital public-service payment boundary

| Budget component | Covers | Does not silently cover | Control |

| Global operating | ordinary hospital operations and certified service obligations | capital, shock reserve, or transition loss | NHSA certification; THDO schedule; audited variance |

| Readiness | ED, trauma, surge, essential on-call and standby capability | unrelated volume incentives | regional need and readiness evidence |

| Essential service-line | OB, psychiatric, ICU, rural inpatient, dialysis, stroke/cardiac, pediatric, safety-net continuity where required | permanent subsidy without review | closure requires regional review and continuity plan |

| Capital | approved replacement, safety, resilience, and capacity projects | routine operating deficit | separate capital ledger and milestone verification |

| Stabilization corridor | time-limited conversion protection | locked-in excess revenue | floor and ceiling; sunset; anti-extraction audit |
Continuity fallbacks

| Failure | Immediate fallback | Accountable authority | Closure evidence |

| Unit unavailable | alternate unit, primary care, mobile/tele route; emergency escalation if needed | RHA/OCDTI | completed encounter or documented safe handoff |

| Specialist capacity exhausted | protected slot, cross-region, tele-specialty, urgent hospital route | NSAA/RHA | accepted route and completion timestamp |

| Payment rail outage | provisional payment and queued replay | THDO/NCCA | settlement and reconciliation |

| Medication/formulary migration failure | continuity bridge unless safety-reviewed substitution/restriction | PCU/PDCO/MARB | fill, substitution consent/review, or appeal disposition |

| Hospital service instability | stabilization corridor, staffing/capacity plan, regional transfer plan | NHSA/HESSO/RHA | service restored or approved continuity transfer |

| Record unavailable | local continuity dataset, patient-provided evidence, failover query, later reconciliation | HCCA/NHRA | record merge and provenance-preserving correction |
CARE SAFETY RULE  No routing or productivity objective may delay emergency escalation, suppress a red flag, or leave an abnormal result without a named follow-up owner. AI may assist, but an accountable human retains every high-stakes decision.
4.7 Information Architecture View
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: A national system cannot coordinate care or protect rights without a defined record, identity, consent, interoperability, cybersecurity, and correction architecture. Why this structure: Each view isolates one stakeholder concern while cross-references preserve the interfaces that make the system operate as a whole. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes information architecture view explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Define the federated information mesh, authoritative data responsibilities, data rights, AI accountability, and controlled interfaces. |

| System entities | AHIRC; NHRA; NHIS; NMPI; NLLHR; NRLS; NCDSO; NAIG; PACP; CIRBAS; HCCA; AICIO; operating/oversight bodies; data subjects. |

| Assumptions | ASM-009, ASM-012–ASM-013, ASM-015, ASM-023, ASM-029–ASM-034. |

| Data / parameters | identity, provenance, consent, segmentation, correction, access, event, rule/formula version, model version, retention, audit, recovery metadata. |

| Requirements / performance | SR-DATA, SR-AI, SR-RGT, SR-EQ, SR-IF; VR-004–013/020–023; TPP-10/11; IF-001–032. |

| Principal risks | Single-database misconception; identity collision; stale rule; unauthorized access; vendor lock-in; silent model change; interface ambiguity; cyber propagation. |

| Simulation implication | Federated state stores and event streams with authority, latency, failure, correction, and provenance semantics. |
The National Health Assurance Information Mesh is a federation of authoritative registries, event streams, governed data products, rules-as-code, audit logs, and human exception review. Federation means an object has an accountable source and can be discovered and exchanged under common controls; it does not mean every datum is copied into one national database.
Table D3-15. Information-mesh layer allocation

| Layer | Information domain | Authority | Authoritative content | Control |

| 1 | Identity | NHIS/NMPI | person/provider/facility identifiers; match confidence | Identity is separate from SSN; correction and collision handling required |

| 2 | Clinical record | NHRA/NLLHR/NRLS | encounters, results, plans, medications, images, provenance | Federated source plus longitudinal view; no uncontrolled central database |

| 3 | Coverage and claims | NEEA/NCCA/PCU | eligibility, benefit, claim, pharmacy, payment status | Purpose-limited; decision and correction history retained |

| 4 | Rules as code | NCCA/NHASB | benefit, routing, payment, formula, version, authority | Every operational rule maps to human-readable authority and Formula Registry |

| 5 | Drug/device/supply ledger | AMDDT | formulary, price, inventory, shortage, substitute, quality release | No opaque PBM control; shortage and access classes visible |

| 6 | Hospital budget ledger | NHSA/HFASB/THDO | budget, readiness, capital, service line, variance, payment | Operating, capital, reserve, and transition ledgers remain distinct |

| 7 | Workforce registry | NHWB/NHWECA | credential, role, vacancy, training, obligation, placement | Scope and staffing uses are bounded and auditable |

| 8 | Quality/safety/appeals | NHAC/NPSMIB/PROO | decision record, complaint, safety event, appeal, remedy | Independent access; nonpunitive reporting and due process protected |

| 9 | Analytics/research | SRAE/NHASB | governed datasets, queries, model outputs, reproducibility | Privacy-preserving enclave; approved purpose and disclosure review |

| 10 | Public transparency | PRTO/CHAO/NHASB | approved metrics, methods, uncertainty, conflicts, timeliness | Suppression and privacy metadata travel with each result |

| Public transparency | public/oversight | PRTO publication with definitions, uncertainty, suppression, and version | CHAO/NHASB | publication_state; timeliness; completeness |

| Class | Use | Examples | Accountable control |

HARD AI RULE  No AI system may be the final authority for denial of covered care, non-referral to a specialist, emergency non-escalation, long-term care reduction, benefit termination, or high-stakes clinical diagnosis. Model version, input provenance, output, human reviewer, action, and contest path must be reconstructable.

4.8 Financial Architecture View
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Collecting revenue and promising benefits do not by themselves move money to pharmacies, clinicians, and hospitals; obligation, reserve, and disbursement roles must be separated. Why this structure: Each view isolates one stakeholder concern while cross-references preserve the interfaces that make the system operate as a whole. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes financial architecture view explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Separate legal obligation, revenue, reserve, disbursement, operating, capital, transition, residual-private, and patient-paid flows. |

| System entities | Congress; Treasury/IRS/THDO; NHA Trust; NHETF; HFASB; DNHA/NCCA; NHSA; NHTCA; PPCO; providers; households; employers. |

| Assumptions | ASM-015, ASM-017–ASM-019, ASM-026–ASM-032, ASM-034–ASM-035. |

| Data / parameters | CP-TOT, CP-POP, CP-FIN, CP-TR, CP-OFF; obligation, receipt, transfer, balance, draw, payment, cost-view and incidence fields. |

| Requirements / performance | PR-CST; SR-PAY/COV/HOSP/LAW/IF; KPP-C; VR-009/017/019/024/025/027. |

| Principal risks | Double count; reserve-as-cost; transfer-as-revenue; public/private boundary error; impoundment; payment delay; fiscal incidence confusion. |

| Simulation implication | Multi-ledger accounting with explicit stocks, flows, authority, payer/payee, timing, view, and reconciliation equations. |
The financial architecture distinguishes who authorizes an obligation, who holds a reserve, who executes payment, who operates a service, and which cost view is being reported. A transfer between public accounts is not new national health cost. A reserve balance is a stock, while a contribution or draw is a flow. Transition and mature operating costs may not book the same event.
Table D3-19. Financial ledger and authority allocation

| Ledger / view | Accountable authority | Contents | Verifier | Boundary control |

| Core entitlement authorization | ARCH-NHA-TRUST | certified covered-care obligations | ARCH-HFASB / ARCH-CHAO | Not a reserve or an operating agency budget |

| Operating stabilization | ARCH-NHETF | temporary operating stabilization and equalization | ARCH-HFASB / ARCH-NHASB | Stock balance; draws are not annual cost unless consumed |

| Shock reserve | ARCH-NHETF | specified recession, emergency, or revenue shock | ARCH-HFASB / ARCH-CHAO | Contribution, balance, draw, and replenishment are separate events |

| Permanent endowment | ARCH-NHETF | long-horizon resilience and authorized earnings | ARCH-HFASB / ARCH-CHAO | Principal and earnings governed separately |

| Treasury disbursement | ARCH-THDO | provider, pharmacy, hospital, and other certified payments | ARCH-CHAO / ARCH-A1-HCAC | Execution rail; cannot change benefit or obligation |

| Hospital operating | ARCH-NHSA | global operating budget | ARCH-HAAO / ARCH-NHASB | Separate from capital, readiness, and transition stabilization |

| Hospital capital | ARCH-NHSA | approved replacement and expansion | ARCH-HAAO / ARCH-CHAO | Capital stock/flow not mixed with operating budget |

| Transition | ARCH-NHTCA | incremental, time-limited conversion costs | ARCH-NHASB / ARCH-CHAO | One event ID; no double count in operating ledger |

| Residual private | ARCH-PPCO | certified supplemental/substitute/administrative spending | ARCH-NHAC / ARCH-HFASB | Reported in total-system view; excluded only by explicit view rule |

| Patient paid | ARCH-NCCA | noncovered or permitted residual patient payment | ARCH-NHAC | Covered-care billing violations tracked separately |
Controlled fund and payment sequence
Congress creates the entitlement, tax/receipt authorities, mandatory payment classification, trust/reserve purposes, and fallback duties.
HFASB certifies obligations, revenue sufficiency, reserve ratios, and stabilizer conditions using versioned assumptions.
Revenue enters the authorized financing structure; transfers among NHA Trust, NHETF accounts, or Treasury are recorded without creating duplicate national cost.
NCCA, PCU, NHSA, or another authorized program authority certifies a payable obligation within its legal domain.
THDO executes the certified payment and returns timestamped settlement/rejection records; it may not change the underlying benefit, price, or eligibility decision.
NHASB and CHAO reconcile obligations, receipts, transfers, balances, payments, and exceptions; NHAC and the Article I court protect individual/provider remedies.
TOTAL-SYSTEM VIEW  C_total = C_public_operating + C_residual_private + C_patient_paid + C_transition_incremental − C_duplicate_offsets
All terms require a common year, price basis, population/service boundary, and booking rule. Reserve contributions/draws and intergovernmental transfers remain visible but are not automatically added to consumption cost.
RECONCILIATION  opening_balance + receipts + transfers_in − payments − transfers_out = closing_balance
Every ledger event has an event ID, authority, payer, payee, amount, time, cost view, and source. Failed reconciliation produces an Indeterminate fiscal result and blocks dependent phase gates.
Table D3-20. Financial control points

| Control point | Owner | Independent check | Failure response |

| Obligation certification | HFASB / program authority | NHASB / CHAO | hold gate; publish variance; corrective financing plan |

| Disbursement execution | THDO | CHAO / Article I court | failover rail; provisional payment; enforceable order |

| Covered-care patient billing | NCCA | NHAC | stop collection; refund; sanction; appeal/remedy |

| Hospital budget/service line | NHSA | HAAO / NHASB | stabilization/corrective plan; anti-extraction action |

| Transition booking | NHTCA | NHASB / CHAO | reclassify duplicate; recover; update transition envelope |

| Residual private role | PPCO | NHAC / HFASB | decertify, refund, anti-duplication enforcement |

| Revenue/reserve sufficiency | HFASB / Treasury | CHAO / NHASB | specified stabilizer/reserve action; no silent benefit cut |
COST CONTROL  The mature $4.75T/year central assumption, $4.30T–$5.25T range, $1.2T–$2.0T transition envelope, and $4.90T–$5.05T first-decade range remain controlling framework assumptions. D3 does not turn the unreconciled per-capita or GDP targets into baselines.
4.9 Legal Architecture View
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Entitlements, duties, preemption, appeals, anti-impoundment protection, and fallback authority must be legally connected or operational promises can be defeated by procedural gaps. Why this structure: Each view isolates one stakeholder concern while cross-references preserve the interfaces that make the system operate as a whole. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes legal architecture view explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Allocate legal authority, federal/state/regional/tribal boundaries, appeal sequence, anti-sabotage controls, fallback, and remedy. |

| System entities | Congress; DNHA; NHAC; NHASB; CHAO; Treasury/THDO; Article I court; RHAs; states; tribal nations; regulated private actors. |

| Assumptions | ASM-003–ASM-006, ASM-009–ASM-014, ASM-018, ASM-024, ASM-029–ASM-034. |

| Data / parameters | statutory authority, duty, preemption, compact, delegation, vacancy, impoundment, appeal, order, fallback, sunset, legal-shock state. |

| Requirements / performance | SR-ARCH/LAW/RGT/EQ/ADP; PR-SCH/TRN; VR-019/021–026. |

| Principal risks | Unconstitutional structure; impoundment; vacancy; preemption conflict; forum delay; unenforceable duty; sovereignty breach; overbroad delegation. |

| Simulation implication | Authority and legal-shock state change which actions are available; fallback matrices preserve core functions after adverse events. |
This is an architectural allocation, not statutory language or a legal opinion. Section 9 will specify conforming amendments, appointment/removal rules, jurisdiction, causes of action, preemption, severability, appropriations classification, and fallback text. Section 4 establishes the functions that the later legal design must make executable.
Table D3-21. Legal authority and boundary allocation

| Authority domain | Legal source / owner | Operational allocation | Review / remedy | Hardening boundary |

| Entitlement and benefit | Congress | mandatory coverage and covered-care obligation | DNHA/NCCA implements; NHAC reviews rights; Article I court remedies | No silent executive benefit withdrawal |

| Appropriation/disbursement | Congress/Treasury | mandatory payment authority and THDO rail | CHAO monitors interference; court can compel lawful payment | Anti-impoundment and automatic fallback required |

| Rights/privacy/safety | Congress/NHAC | patient rights, privacy, safety, explanation, appeal | HRPO/NOPRSL/PROO administer; court reviews | Independent from DNHA operations |

| Regional administration | DNHA/RHA | national floors with regional execution | state/tribal compact where agreed; direct federal fallback | Compact cannot waive core rights or tribal sovereignty |

Baseline claims and appeals sequence

| Stage | Function | Time/urgency control | Decision owner | Escalation |

| 0. Complete decision record | facts, rule, evidence, urgency, alternative, human reviewer, appeal path | at decision/notice | operating authority | missing record favors provisional protection |

| 1. Operational reconsideration | correct clerical/factual/rule application error | urgency-specific | separate reviewer within operator | NHAC rights review |

| 2. Rights/ombudsman review | usability, rights, safety, interim relief, complete packet | expedited; emergency relief available | NHAC/PROO | Article I court |

| 3. Optional NAT | only if statute shows it accelerates independent merits review | must not delay court access or urgent relief | ARCH-NAT if retained | Article I court |

| 4. Article I review | enforceable patient/provider/payment/anti-impoundment remedy | expedited by claim class | ARCH-A1-HCAC | appellate review as statute provides |

| 5. Remedy execution/learning | stay, reversal, service/payment order, correction, systemic learning | tracked to completion | operator/THDO; oversight monitors | contempt/enforcement and adaptation review |
OI DISPOSITION  OI-004 is bounded: a mandatory National Appeals Tribunal is not part of the baseline critical path. It may be retained in Section 9 only if it does not add delay, restrict Article I access, or weaken provisional relief. OI-003 is bounded by the NHA Trust/NHETF/THDO function split.
Legal fallback principles
Core entitlement and certified obligations remain mandatory notwithstanding annual appropriations conflict, subject to constitutional design in Section 9.
Vacancy, missed appointment, or executive nonfeasance activates succession or direct statutory fallback rather than suspending patient/provider rights.
If a compact fails or is absent, direct federal administration preserves national floors; tribal compacts and trust duties remain direct federal obligations.
If a formula, pilot, vendor, or technology fails, NHASB may use only the bounded repair tier authorized for that failure, with notice, expiration, review, and rollback.
Severability and fallback design must preserve coverage, lawful payment, continuity, rights, records, and review after an adverse court ruling wherever legally possible.
4.10 Verification and Assurance View
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Self-reported compliance is insufficient for a system of this scale; every critical claim needs an independent method, evidence owner, acceptance rule, and remedy for failure. Why this structure: Each view isolates one stakeholder concern while cross-references preserve the interfaces that make the system operate as a whole. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes verification and assurance view explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Allocate verification requirements, methods, evidence, independence, phase-gate effect, and result semantics. |

| System entities | Requirement owners; NHASB; NHAC; CHAO; HAAO; HRPO; NPSMIB; HFASB; Article I court; independent audit/testing bodies. |

| Assumptions | ASM-015, ASM-020, ASM-029–ASM-034. |

| Data / parameters | requirement version, method, entry/exit criteria, evidence artifact, sample/coverage, verifier, timestamp, result, exception, corrective action. |

| Principal risks | Self-verification; cherry-picked evidence; missing denominator; stale version; unverifiable target; suppressed adverse result; gate override. |

| Simulation implication | Verification events consume evidence and emit Pass/Fail/Indeterminate/Not Applicable plus confidence, limitations, and gate consequence. |
Assurance is independent enough to challenge the operator, but close enough to the data and workflow to reproduce the result. An operating dashboard, contractor attestation, or model output can be evidence; none is automatically verification. A failed or indeterminate safety/gate result cannot be overwritten by an aggregate success score.

Verification result and gate semantics

| Result | Meaning | Allowed gate treatment |

| Pass | controlled criterion satisfied by sufficient, current, independently acceptable evidence | may satisfy the linked gate condition |

| Fail | criterion not satisfied or prohibited condition observed | blocks/reverts dependent capability; corrective action required |

| Indeterminate | evidence missing, stale, irreproducible, conflicting, or authority unclear | cannot count as Pass; blocks a mandatory gate |

| Not Applicable | controlled applicability rule excludes this requirement for the case | requires recorded rule and verifier acceptance |
ASSURANCE INDEPENDENCE  requirement_owner ≠ independent_verifier
A supporting contributor may participate in evidence production, but the accountable owner may not be the sole verifier of its own phase-gate or safety-critical result.
