9.2.2 Transition sequencing
Inventory every function and legal dependency before enactment implementation; assign a durable custodian and prohibit unowned legacy records, appeals or liabilities.
Activate successor authority, funding, systems and remedies before predecessor authority is narrowed; dual-run only where needed and record its cost under the transition ledger.
Migrate populations and providers by certified wave, preserving active treatment, authorizations, pharmacy access, appeal posture and payment liquidity.
Close a legacy function only after record transfer, financial reconciliation, pending-case disposition, workforce treatment and independent Gate 8 evidence.
Retain savings clauses and revival/fallback authority for latent claims, audit, fraud recovery, records correction and judicial orders after operational sunset.
9.3 State, Regional, and Tribal Legal Architecture
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Federal standards must coexist with state delivery roles, regional adaptation, and tribal sovereignty; those relationships cannot be reduced to ordinary preemption. Why this structure: Legal authorities are organized around enforceable dependencies and fallback paths so operational duties do not rest on implied power. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes state, regional, and tribal legal architecture explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Define federal floors, compatible state authority, regional compacts, direct-federal fallback and nation-to-nation tribal pathways. |

| System entities | DNHA; RHA; SRCO; TRTO; states/territories/localities; tribal governments/health authorities; NHTCA |

| Assumptions | Federal law preempts material interference with NHA operation while preserving compatible health, safety, discipline, public-health, supplemental and more-protective rules. |

| Data / parameters | compact obligation, legal authority, funding, service/data allocation, compliance, breach, cure, fallback, tribal approval |

| Requirements / performance | SR-ARCH-008; SR-EQ-008–010; VR-026 |

| Principal risks | RISK-STATE-001; LR-TRIB-001 |

| Simulation implication | Represent jurisdiction-specific rules, compact state, capacity, funding and fallback; simulate refusal/incapacity without assuming service loss. |
The federalism design has three operating modes: cooperative compact administration, federally led regional administration with state/local interfaces, and direct federal fallback. Mode choice changes who administers functions; it does not change the national entitlement, federal payment duty, minimum rights, tribal trust responsibility or continuity floor.
Table D7A-07. State conforming domains

| Domain | State law families | Conforming rule | Fallback |

| Insurance/coverage | Insurance codes; Medicaid/CHIP; state employee plans | Remove conflicting substitute-coverage duties; preserve compatible supplemental and consumer protection | Direct federal enrollment/payment if state action blocks continuity |

| Workforce | Scope of practice; professional licensing | Federal minimum scope/credential pathway plus state health, safety and discipline above the floor | Direct federal credential/facility pathway where permissible |

| Facilities/capacity | CON; hospital/LTC licensing; pharmacy laws | Conform global budgets, public-service charters, unit network and pharmacy access | Federal facility/contract operation and payment conditions |

| Public functions | Public health; vital records; EMS; disability supports | Define data, command, service, funding and emergency interfaces | RHA/direct-federal administration with state cooperation incentives |

| Civil liability/households | Medical debt; tort/malpractice | Conform covered-debt rules, patient remedies, compensation and federal/state cause-of-action boundaries | Federal floor; more-protective compatible state remedy |
9.3.1 Preemption and preserved authority
Federal law preempts a state rule that prevents, frustrates, duplicates or materially interferes with enrollment, coverage, payment, pharmacy access, purchasing, public manufacturing, global budgets, records, participation, federal scope floors or transition continuity.
States retain compatible authority over health, safety, licensure, discipline, public health, supplemental coverage and more-protective rules. Compatibility is tested against operational interference, rights, continuity, cost shifting and data burden.
Disputes use expedited administrative determination and judicial review; the challenged rule remains subject to a continuity order so patients and providers are not forced to absorb the dispute.
A preemption holding narrower than planned activates conditional funding, direct credentials/facilities or direct federal administration rather than automatic benefit or capacity reduction.
9.3.2 Compact schema and fallback
Table D7A-08. Required compact fields

| Field group | Required content |

| identity/authority | parties, geography, legal authority, effective/sunset dates, amendment and dispute forum |

| operating allocation | enrollment, claims, payment, capacity, workforce, public health, data and transition responsibilities |

| funding | maintenance contribution, direct transfers, equalization, allowable use, audit and reconciliation |

| rights/standards | federal floors, more-protective rules, appeals, accessibility, continuity and anti-discrimination |

| data/governance | stewardship, permitted exchange, privacy/segmentation, tribal governance, cybersecurity and retention |

| performance | requirements, KPP/TPP, evidence, reporting, corrective action and phase-gate effects |

| failure/fallback | breach triggers, cure, temporary federal operation, asset/data access, funding continuity and reentry |
9.3.3 Tribal legal architecture
TRIBAL PRINCIPLE  No transition provision may reduce, replace or condition federal trust obligations to tribal nations unless expressly agreed through tribal consultation and statutory consent mechanisms. A state may not veto tribal participation in federally authorized NHA functions.
Provide direct federal–tribal compact and funding pathways, with tribal choice over participation form and no mandatory state intermediary.
Use nation-to-nation consultation and tribal-approved documentation for compact duties; state certification alone cannot verify VR-026.
Preserve tribal data governance, culturally and linguistically appropriate service design, federal facility and workforce duties, and IHS/tribal/urban Indian health interfaces until expressly agreed otherwise.
Define dispute, cure, withdrawal, emergency funding and direct-operation terms without using funding interruption as leverage against a tribal nation.
Track SR-EQ-008 compliance (>=98% compact requirements by P8), direct funding under SR-EQ-009 and state non-veto under SR-EQ-010 as separate results.
9.4 Executive-Branch Hardening
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: A future executive could hollow out the system through vacancies, delayed rules, impoundment, data withholding, or non-enforcement without formally repealing it. Why this structure: Legal authorities are organized around enforceable dependencies and fallback paths so operational duties do not rest on implied power. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes executive-branch hardening explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Make critical coverage, payment, governance, staffing, data and continuity duties resistant to withholding, vacancy, hollowing, regulatory nonfeasance and contractor obstruction. |

| System entities | Congress; THDO/Treasury; DNHA; NHASB; CHAO; A1-HCAC/federal courts; OMB; critical offices |

| Assumptions | Hardening protects lawful continuity and enforceable rights while retaining bounded, transparent adaptation through Title XVIII. |

| Data / parameters | authority/payment clock, staffing/quorum, regulation deadline/default, delay flag, action timestamp, case/remedy, continuity result |

| Requirements / performance | SR-LAW-001–010; TPP-12.1–12.5; VR-019 |

| Principal risks | LR-IMP-001; LR-FB-001 |

| Simulation implication | Inject vacancy, non-issuance, impoundment, data suppression and vendor failure; measure continuity, payment delay, activation time and remedy success. |
Executive hardening is a layered control system. Self-executing duties and defaults keep the service operating; independent evidence detects deviation; standing and expedited forums make rights enforceable; Treasury, escrow and step-in mechanisms restore execution. Hardening cannot authorize secret benefit narrowing or freeze legitimate evidence-based correction.
Table D7A-09. Executive-hardening controls

| ID | Control | Controlled rule/target | Trigger | Remedy/default |

| EH-01 | Statutory entitlement | Core covered benefits and enforceable rights are fixed by statute | Benefit restriction outside statutory process | A1-HCAC/district review; continued lawful default |

| EH-02 | Permanent mandatory appropriations | At least 99.5% of core spending under payment protection by P8 | Missing/withheld discretionary action | Treasury payment duty and judicial enforcement |

| EH-03 | Deemed/default apportionment | Formula-based apportionment occurs when ordinary process fails | Deadline passes without lawful apportionment | Registered default amount; narrower fallback if challenged |

| EH-04 | Direct Treasury disbursement | THDO pays certified obligations without policy repricing | Certified obligation reaches payment clock | Deemed payment/remedy, interest and court order |

| EH-05 | Payment rights/defaults | Clean-claim deemed allowance; provider/hospital/pharmacy rights | Agency fails adjudication/payment clock | Provisional/deemed allowance subject to later reconciliation |

| EH-06 | Vacancy-proof governance | Acting succession; no duty failure for vacancy/quorum; continuity >=99% | Vacancy, no quorum or appointment failure | Delegated statutory actor and automatic duty continuation |

| EH-07 | Staffing/anti-hollowing | Critical-office staffing >=98%; no freeze/RIF below floor; direct hire | Vacancy threshold or prohibited staffing action | Direct-hire and enforceable restoration |

| EH-08 | Oversight and remedies | CHAO oversight; standing; Article I and district-court routes | Delay, suppression, unlawful narrowing or impoundment | 24-hour action initiation; injunction/mandamus/payment relief |

| EH-09 | Systems/data continuity | Public data/systems escrow, continuity contracts, portable records and vendor exit | Operator/vendor refusal, termination or outage | Escrow release, step-in rights and offline operation |

| EH-10 | Anti-regulatory sabotage | Automatic defaults for formulary, budgets, claims, LTC, compensation and reporting | Required regulation missing/invalid/withdrawn | Last lawful or statutory default rule with public notice and repair |

| EH-11 | Anti-impoundment | Automated delay flag and action within 24 hours | Unlawful withholding, deferral, transfer or administrative obstruction | Direct payment, expedited review, personal/office accountability as enacted |

| EH-12 | State/regional fallback | Direct federal administration and continuity contracts are preauthorized | Compact refusal, breach or incapacity threatens service | Temporary federal operation with cure/reentry plan |
9.4.1 Detection-to-remedy workflow
Detect through operational logs, statutory clocks, certified obligations, staffing/quorum records, regulation calendars, public-data completeness, escrow status and complaints—not discretionary self-attestation alone.
Classify the event as lawful adjustment, operational incident, unlawful delay/impoundment, vacancy/nonfeasance, contractor obstruction, data suppression or legal constraint; preserve the evidence package.
Apply the narrowest self-executing continuity default immediately: payment, acting succession, last-lawful/formula rule, escrow release, offline operation or direct-federal function.
For an unlawful delay flag, initiate legal or administrative action within 24 hours under SR-LAW-004 while CHAO/NHASB/NHAC receive notice appropriate to their authority.
Reconcile provisional payments/actions after review without shifting error cost to patients; publish the event, authority, duration, remedy, affected population and corrective result subject to privacy/security limits.
Table D7A-10. Hardening verification package

| Requirement group | Evidence | Pass concept |

| Mandatory payment | statutory/appropriations classification; obligations; apportionment; disbursement logs | >=99.5% core spending protected; lawful payments meet clocks |

| Staffing/vacancy | position roster; succession; quorum; vacancy; service logs | >=98% staffing floor and >=99% critical-function continuity at P8 |

| Anti-impoundment | delay flag; legal assessment; action timestamp; remedy/payment | action initiated <=24 hours and continuity preserved |

| Regulatory default | deadline; applicable default version; notice; output; review | required function operates lawfully without silent narrowing |

| Data/systems | publication log; escrow; vendor access; downtime exercise | no suppression; step-in/offline controls meet service levels |

| Legal coverage | critical-provision inventory; primary/fallback authority; exercise result | >=99% legal contingency coverage by P8 |
9.5 Legal Contingency and Fallback Matrix
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Courts may limit one authority or remedy; predetermined severability and fallback paths prevent a single adverse ruling from collapsing unrelated protections. Why this structure: Legal authorities are organized around enforceable dependencies and fallback paths so operational duties do not rest on implied power. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes legal contingency and fallback matrix explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| System entities | Provision owner; DOJ; Congress; Treasury; DNHA; NHASB/CHAO; operational fallback owner |

| Assumptions | Fallbacks are scoped to the lost authority, do not evade final judgments, and undergo public/legal, fiscal, rights, equity, operational and sunset review. |

| Requirements / performance | SR-LAW-009; VR-019/022/025 |

| Principal risks | RISK-LEGAL-001; LR-FB-001; SCN-LEGAL |

| Simulation implication | Run primary and fallback branches with correlated litigation timing, injunction scope, activation delay, capacity/yield substitution, rights and distributional effects. |
A legal contingency is operational only when the substitute has authority, owner, funding, people, systems, data, contracts, communications and a tested activation path. The source package specifies eleven controlled fallback families. Exact legal instruments, replacement yields and recovery-time objectives remain open pending specialized analysis.

Table D7A-12. Legal states

| State | Name | Entry condition | Required posture |

| LS-0 | operative | Primary authority effective; no material challenge | Normal monitoring |

| LS-3 | invalidated | Controlling judgment or statutory repeal removes primary authority | Activate certified substitute; record distributional/operational delta |

9.5.2 Fallback activation contract
Provision owner and counsel authenticate the controlling event, affected provisions, geography/population, duration, appeal posture and prohibited conduct; speculative challenge alone does not silently curtail service.
NHASB/CHAO independently records the primary-function loss, selected fallback, legal basis, expected activation lag, fiscal/capacity substitution, affected rights and equity/distributional effects.
Operational owner activates only the scoped substitute needed to preserve the function, publishes required notice, protects pending cases and records, and maintains a return/reconciliation ledger.
The system monitors legal RTO, payment/access continuity, revenue or capacity replacement, administrative burden, privacy, safety, workforce and public trust; threshold breach escalates to a higher fallback or legislative repair.
Fallback authority expires or transitions under its statutory rule after controlling law, replacement legislation or repaired authority stabilizes; retrospective review records costs, harms, benefits and permanent design changes.

10. Risk and Failure Modes
10.1 Risk Register
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: The framework's largest threats cross legal, fiscal, workforce, operational, data, and legitimacy domains; they require named owners and observable triggers. Why this structure: Risk analysis separates hazard identification, causal failure analysis, and adversarial exercises because each detects a different class of weakness. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes risk register explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Establish a living, traceable register connecting failure modes to owners, indicators, controls, fallbacks, verification and simulation propagation. |

| System entities | Architecture owners; NHASB; CHAO; NHAC/NOPRSL; NHTCA; phase-gate authorities |

| Assumptions | Risk is assessed at national and stratified regional/population levels; risk cannot be closed solely because the national mean passes. |

| Data / parameters | risk ID/version, cause/effect, indicators, S/O/D, velocity, correlations, controls, fallback, RTO, residual acceptance |

| Requirements / performance | VR-025; allocated SR/KPP/TPP; phase gates |

| Principal risks | all RISK records; common-cause and blind-spot risk |

| Simulation implication | Instantiate risk events with detection, control, propagation, fallback and recovery states; retain raw and residual measures. |
The register is an operational control plane rather than a static list. A record moves through IDENTIFIED, ASSESSED, CONTROLLED, ACTIVE, RECOVERING, ACCEPTED or CLOSED states. Closure requires evidence that the initiating condition and residual exposure are within approved bounds; a successful fallback does not erase the initiating failure or patient harm.

| RISK-FIN-001 | Wealth financing underperforms | IRS / HFASB | receipt shortfall; forecast error; reserve drawdown | tax stabilizer; enforcement; progressive threshold expansion; legal fallback | revenue sufficiency; reserves; burden; phase gates | month / fiscal year | KPP-C5/C7/C8; VR-024 |

| RISK-AI-001 | AI routing causes unsafe or biased decisions | AICIO / NOPRSL | adverse events; drift; override disparity; equity gap | suspend model; human review; rollback/retraining; patient remedy | safety; equity; access; legitimacy | minutes / 24 h | KPP-D6; KPP-E2; TPP-11.4–TPP-11.6; VR-006/007/011 |

| RISK-CYBER-001 | Cyberattack disrupts records, claims, or pharmacy | HCCA | downtime; intrusion signals; integrity mismatch | failover; isolation; offline continuity; emergency manual operation | multi-rail continuity; privacy; safety; payment | minutes / 24 h | TPP-11.1–TPP-11.3; TPP-10; VR-008 |

| RISK-EXEC-001 | Executive sabotage, impoundment, or hollowing | CHAO / A1-HCAC | delayed funds; staffing freeze; withheld data; missing rules | anti-impoundment action; statutory defaults; succession; court order | coverage/payment; governance; public trust | 24 h / 7 days | SR-LAW-001–010; VR-019 |

| RISK-STATE-001 | State resistance impairs transition | SRCO / RHA | compact refusal; data blockage; licensing obstruction | conditional funding; federal fallback administration; direct facilities/credentials | regional continuity; workforce; public health | week / 90 days | SR-ARCH-008; SR-EQ-010; VR-026 |

| RISK-WF-001 | Workforce shortages exceed plan | NHWB / NHWECA | vacancies; overtime; burnout; unsafe ratios | scope expansion; training acceleration; premium pay; team redesign | capacity; safety; wait; cost; retention | month / 2 years | TPP-7.1–TPP-7.5; TPP-7; VR-025 |

| RISK-LEGAL-001 | Court invalidates major financing or governance tool | NHASB / CONG | injunction; adverse ruling; counsel risk escalation | automatic scoped legal fallback; expedited review; continuity funding/operation | fiscal/legal resilience; access; burden | event / 90 days | SR-LAW-009; VR-019/022 |

| RISK-TRUST-001 | Public trust collapses | NOPRSL / NHASB | trust index drop; complaints; opt-out/avoidance; misinformation | confidence repair review; transparent explanation; service redesign; independent inquiry | utilization; adherence; legitimacy; transition | quarter / 1 year | KPP-TRUST1; VR-028 |

| RISK-DATA-001 | Data migration errors harm continuity | DMRCO / NHRA | missing authorization; identity/record mismatch; duplicate or lost record | provisional coverage; reconciliation; manual review; correction and notice | active treatment; safety; appeal; privacy | hour / 30 days | KPP-T1; KPP-T2; VR-015 |

| RISK-PMC-001 | Public manufacturing quality failure | PMC / AMDDT | failed batch; deviation; recall; shortage signal | quarantine/recall; dual-source procurement; emergency purchasing; CAPA | product safety; medication access; cost; trust | minutes / 30 days | KPP-T2; VR-018 |
10.1.1 Risk-record schema

| Field group | Required content |

| identity | risk ID, title, version, status, owner, accountable executive, affected ARCH/IF/PH/SCN objects |

| causal structure | initiating cause, enabling condition, dependency, failure mode, local effect, system/patient/cost/equity/legal effects |

| measurement | indicator ID, source, cadence, threshold, confidence, stratification, leading/lagging designation and missing-data rule |

| assessment | severity, probability/occurrence, detectability, velocity, duration, correlation/common cause and uncertainty |

| response | preventive control, detective control, mitigation, fallback, decision authority, resources, trigger, RTO/RPO and escalation |

| assurance | requirement/VR, exercise/test, evidence, verifier, residual risk, acceptance authority, review date and closure criteria |

| simulation | state transition, injected parameters, affected modules/interfaces, propagation rule, recovery curve and outputs |
10.1.2 Governance and escalation
The operating owner maintains controls and evidence; NHASB challenges model/formula and systemic risk; NHAC/NOPRSL protects rights and safety; CHAO oversees statutory/executive performance; gate authority blocks progression when evidence is insufficient.
A threshold breach creates an incident/risk-event record and cannot be suppressed by aggregation, delayed reporting, contractor classification or a change in metric definition.
Patient safety, entitlement/payment continuity, tribal duties, ordinary-household burden and prohibited discrimination are constraints, not risk-score tradeables.
Risks sharing data, vendors, workforce, Treasury/payment rails, legal authority or public confidence receive a common-cause group and correlated scenario treatment.
Acceptance identifies residual risk, affected populations, duration, compensating controls, verifier, accountable authority and review/expiry; acceptance is not closure.
10.2 Failure-Mode and Effects Analysis
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: A risk label does not show how a component fails, who is harmed, how failure is detected, or which control breaks the causal chain. Why this structure: Risk analysis separates hazard identification, causal failure analysis, and adversarial exercises because each detects a different class of weakness. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes failure-mode and effects analysis explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Expand the source seed into a reproducible FMEA while preserving qualitative rationale and avoiding unsupported probability claims. |

| System entities | Risk owners; safety/quality teams; NHASB; independent verifiers; model team |

| Assumptions | S/O/D use 1–5 ordinal scales. RPN=S×O×D is a triage index only; severity-5 items and rights/continuity constraints receive priority regardless of RPN. |

| Data / parameters | S, O, D, RPN, uncertainty, rationale, controls, residual score, evidence, test, RTO/RPO |

| Requirements / performance | VR-002–007/019/025; risk-specific VR |

| Principal risks | ranking bias; false precision; hidden common cause; control overstatement |

| Simulation implication | Use distributions/sensitivity around ordinal mappings; compare raw and post-control states; never treat RPN as probability. |
Table D7B-04. Provisional ordinal scale

| Dimension | Score | Controlled interpretation |

| Severity S | 1 | Negligible; no care disruption; localized reversible administrative effect |

| Severity S | 2 | Minor; short localized delay; no expected clinical harm |

| Severity S | 3 | Moderate; material access/payment impact or reversible patient harm |

| Severity S | 4 | Major; serious harm, regional disruption, substantial fiscal/legal effect |

| Severity S | 5 | Catastrophic; deaths/severe harm, national continuity failure or existential legal/fiscal loss |

| Occurrence O | 1 | Remote within scenario horizon |

| Occurrence O | 2 | Unlikely |

| Occurrence O | 3 | Plausible |

| Occurrence O | 4 | Likely |

| Occurrence O | 5 | Frequent/expected without control |

| Detectability D | 1 | Near-certain early detection with operational telemetry |

| Detectability D | 2 | High detection before material harm |

| Detectability D | 3 | Mixed; detected near onset |

| Detectability D | 4 | Low; often detected after harm |

| Detectability D | 5 | Very low; latent, suppressed or not measurable |
FMEA SCORING RULE  RPN supports triage, not acceptance. It is non-interval ordinal arithmetic, may hide a catastrophic severity score, and is sensitive to subjective detectability. Report S, O and D separately with rationale and uncertainty.

| RISK-PHARM-001 | 5 | 3 | 1 | 15 | Medication interruption can be acute; real-time signals | offline/emergency-fill drill |

| RISK-UNIT-001 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 36 | Slow capacity failure may hide in averages | regional gate and demand stress |

| RISK-SPEC-001 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 48 | Queue propagation and silent under-referral | specialty surge exercise |

| RISK-HOSP-001 | 5 | 3 | 3 | 45 | Service closure can lag budget signal | budget-corridor stress |

| RISK-FIN-001 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 24 | Monthly receipts visible; effects can compound | revenue/reserve stress |

| RISK-AI-001 | 5 | 3 | 4 | 60 | Bias/safety harm can evade aggregate metrics | shadow/rollback/equity test |

10.2.1 FMEA workflow
Decompose each risk into one or more failure modes at the level where cause, effect, control and verification differ; avoid a single score for unrelated mechanisms.
Score the uncontrolled or current-control state, record evidence and uncertainty, identify safety/rights constraints, then evaluate preventive, detective, mitigative and fallback controls separately.
Model control independence and common-cause failure. A control that depends on the failed rail, vendor, data source, workforce or legal authority receives no automatic credit.
Exercise the fallback, measure detection/decision/activation/recovery time and patient/equity/cost effects, then rescore residual S/O/D without reducing severity merely because compensation is available.
Prioritize severity-5, high-velocity, low-detectability and cross-module risks; send unresolved gate-critical findings to corrective action and block affected phase progression under VR-025.
10.3 Red-Team Scenarios
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Nominal-case analysis hides compound failures; adversarial scenarios are needed to test simultaneous shocks, malicious behavior, and delayed detection. Why this structure: Risk analysis separates hazard identification, causal failure analysis, and adversarial exercises because each detects a different class of weakness. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes red-team scenarios explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Define adversarial compound scenarios that test coupled controls, fallback operability, equity effects and recovery rather than isolated nominal failures. |

| System entities | Independent red team; NHASB; NHAC/NOPRSL; CHAO; NHTCA; operators; legal/cyber/safety specialists |

| Assumptions | Exercises protect patients and live operations; destructive testing uses sandbox/digital-twin environments unless separately authorized and controlled. |

| Data / parameters | scenario, threat/failure sequence, initial state, injections, observables, controls disabled, stop rules, required outputs, remediation/retest |

| Requirements / performance | SR-ADP; SR-LAW; VR-022/025; RISK/SCN |

| Principal risks | unsafe testing; unrealistic omniscience; omitted common cause; defensive gaming |

| Simulation implication | Execute event sequences across modules with seeded hidden facts, delayed detection, partial observability and after-action correction. |
The red team tests whether the architecture still protects people when several assumptions fail at once. Scenarios deliberately include conflicting objectives, incomplete data, delayed recognition and control dependencies. Teams must not assume perfect coordination, unlimited surge staff, instantaneous legal authority or identical fallback capacity.

| Scenario | Name | Compound injection | Risk linkage | Expected controls | Required outputs |

| SCN-RT-01 | Payment cascade | Cyberattack disables claims + pharmacy while provider liquidity is low | RISK-CYBER/CLAIMS/PHARM | offline continuity; provisional payment; emergency fills; reconciliation | patient interruptions; unpaid obligations; recovery time; duplicate/improper payment |

| SCN-RT-02 | Capacity squeeze | Unit network underbuild + workforce shortage + BH surge + rural stress | RISK-UNIT/WF/SPEC | gate delay; mobile/team capacity; urgency protection; transport support | waits; ED load; unmet need; equity; burnout; cost |

| SCN-RT-03 | Hospital destabilization | Underbudgeted hospitals + drug shortage + workforce attrition | RISK-HOSP/PMC/WF | corridor payment; service-line protection; dual source; premium staffing | closure risk; diversion; mortality proxy; reserve draw |

| SCN-RT-04 | Fiscal-legal shock | Wealth receipts fall as court narrows financing and OMB bypass | RISK-FIN/LEGAL/EXEC | legal tax fallback; reserve; court-ordered payment; stabilizer | revenue gap; burden incidence; payment continuity; reserve months |

| SCN-RT-05 | Federalism fracture | Hostile states block compact, data and credentials during migration | RISK-STATE/DATA/WF | conditional funding; direct administration; federated data; direct credentials | coverage gap; access; legal RTO; state/tribal disparity |

| SCN-RT-06 | Algorithmic inequity | AI under-refers a protected group while dashboards average the effect away | RISK-AI/TRUST | stratified detection; suspension; human re-review; restitution; disclosure | harm; delayed diagnosis; appeal; trust; correction time |

| SCN-RT-07 | Migration harm | Legacy authorizations and cancer-treatment records fail to transfer | RISK-DATA/CLAIMS | provisional coverage/payment; manual clinical reconciliation; ombudsman | missed treatment; appeal; safety event; cost and closeout time |

| SCN-RT-08 | Manufacturing recall | PMC batch failure coincides with external supplier shortage | RISK-PMC/PHARM | recall; emergency procurement; therapeutic substitution; allocation transparency | shortage exposure; adverse events; price/cost; trust |

| SCN-RT-09 | Legitimacy attack | Withheld performance data + service delays + coordinated misinformation | RISK-EXEC/TRUST | data escrow; independent publication; confidence repair; service correction | trust; utilization avoidance; complaints; recovery |

| SCN-RT-10 | Pandemic transition collision | Public-health surge during coverage conversion and workforce shortage | RISK-WF/CLAIMS/UNIT/HOSP | transition pause; surge funding; flexible capacity; continuity defaults | mortality proxy; access; staffing; cost; phase delay |
10.3.1 Exercise contract
Freeze the baseline configuration, formulas, data and assumptions; document the threat model, protected populations, safety boundary, no-go actions and abort authority.
Inject events through real module interfaces and clocks. Withhold some causal facts from operators to test telemetry, escalation and independent verification.
Measure recognition, decision, activation and recovery separately; record coverage/treatment/payment interruptions, harms, burden, equity, fiscal/capacity effects and communications.
Do not credit a named fallback unless the exercise demonstrates authority, staffing, data, assets, contracts, funding, communications and reconciliation within the proposed RTO.
Publish a protected/public after-action pair, assign corrective actions and deadlines, retest material findings, and update RISK/FMEA/SCN/formula/phase-gate records under change control.
11. Simulation Specification
11.1 Simulation Objective
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: The simulation must answer a defined policy question rather than merely reproduce the framework's own assumptions. Why this structure: The simulation specification separates model purpose, state, parameters, scenarios, outputs, and input validation so results can be reproduced and contested. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes simulation objective explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Define the comparison, decision uses, boundaries, uncertainty and validation conditions for evaluating NHA against continuation of the existing U.S. system. |

| System entities | Model sponsor; NHASB; CHAO; framework owners; independent validation team; public users |

| Assumptions | The simulation is comparative and decision-supporting, not a deterministic forecast, clinical decision tool, budget score or substitute for legal/actuarial review. |

| Data / parameters | comparator version, horizon, price basis, geography/population, scenario, parameter distributions, validation, outputs, provenance |

| Requirements / performance | PR-CST; KPP/TPP; VR-001–005/024/025 |

| Principal risks | baseline bias; causal overclaim; missing data; unmodeled behavior; misuse |

| Simulation implication | Run paired scenarios with common exogenous draws where appropriate; report distributions, differences, constraint failures and sensitivity. |
The simulation shall compare the existing U.S. healthcare system with the National Health Assurance Framework across total and transition-adjusted cost, access, safety, quality, equity, workforce, household and employer burden, provider stability, fiscal sustainability, transition continuity, legal resilience and public trust. It must expose tradeoffs and failure conditions, not optimize to a preferred conclusion.
Table D7B-07. Simulation objectives

| ID | Objective | Decision question | Principal output |

| OBJ-01 | Comparative performance | Compare existing U.S. system and NHA across cost, access, safety, quality, equity, workforce, household/employer burden, provider stability, fiscal sustainability, transition, legal resilience and trust | annual and quarterly distributions by national/regional/population dimensions |

| OBJ-02 | Design adequacy | Test whether architecture and capacity meet stakeholder needs and controlled KPP/TPP/requirements under baseline and stress | pass/fail with margin and binding constraint |

| OBJ-03 | Implementation safety | Estimate transition failures, dual-run cost, liquidity, active-treatment continuity and phase-gate readiness | failure counts/rates, cost, recovery and gate result |

| OBJ-04 | Fiscal sustainability | Reconcile total-system cost, public outlay, receipts, reserves, incidence and stabilizer/legal-fallback behavior | cost/receipt/reserve/burden paths with uncertainty |

| OBJ-05 | Risk propagation | Trace single and compound failures through interfaces, controls, fallbacks and recovery | causal event log, downstream effects and residual risk |

| OBJ-06 | Decision support | Identify robust policies, capacity margins, trigger thresholds and research priorities—not produce a single-point prediction | scenario dominance, sensitivity, tradeoffs and value of information |
11.1.1 Comparison contract
Version both comparators. Existing-system continuation includes policy, demographic, price, capacity and behavioral assumptions; NHA includes phase, gate, capacity, financing, transition and legal states.
Use real 2024 dollars for controlled economic comparisons and retain nominal cash views where financing/operations require them; reconcile total-system cost, public outlay, transfers and reserves.
Align population, morbidity, macroeconomic and external shock draws across comparators where conceptually common; keep policy-responsive behaviors endogenous and separately documented.
Report national results with regional and population distributions. A favorable mean cannot offset a binding safety, rights, tribal, rural, disability, language or ordinary-household constraint.
Separate specification targets, calibrated parameters, external observations, assumptions, inferred quantities and model outputs; attach provenance, version, uncertainty and owner to each input.
Validate through conservation/unit tests, historical comparator fit, cross-module reconciliation, extreme cases, face validity, sensitivity and independent reproduction; publish non-use limitations.
NON-USE RULE  The model must not be used to deny individual care, generate patient-specific clinical recommendations, conceal uncertainty, certify legal validity, or convert an uncalibrated scenario into a budget forecast.
11.2 Model Modules
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Coverage, demand, capacity, workforce, payment, supply, finance, rights, and transition interact dynamically; one aggregate equation cannot represent those feedbacks. Why this structure: The simulation specification separates model purpose, state, parameters, scenarios, outputs, and input validation so results can be reproduced and contested. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes model modules explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Partition the simulation into explicit, testable modules with controlled state ownership, interfaces, time steps and conservation/reconciliation rules. |

| System entities | Nineteen model modules; data stewards; architecture owners; model integration and validation teams |

| Assumptions | Hybrid implementation is permitted. Module boundaries follow causal/operational responsibility, not agency charts alone; shared variables have one authoritative owner. |

| Data / parameters | module ID/version, state/input/output, unit, grain, update rule, dependencies, calibration, uncertainty, tests |

| Requirements / performance | ARCH/IF/DATA/CP/KPP/TPP/RISK/SCN allocations |

| Principal risks | double counting; algebraic loops; inconsistent clocks; hidden shared state; nonconvergence |

| Simulation implication | Implement modules as replaceable components with typed contracts, event logs, deterministic seeds where applicable and integration tests. |

11.2.1 Module integration rules

| Rule | Controlled treatment |

| time | Annual core step; quarterly/monthly/event substeps for transition, claims, queues, receipts, cyber, legal and surge dynamics |

| population | Microsimulation or stratified cells; preserve weights and protected/vulnerable stratification where lawful/ethical |

| capacity | Stock-flow and queue constraints; no service, saving or access improvement without staffed/equipped capacity |

| money | Real-2024 economic cost, nominal cash, obligation, outlay, receipt, transfer and reserve are separate views |

| behavior | Explicit response for patients, employers, providers, workforce, suppliers, states and taxpayers; uncertain parameters scenario-tested |

| causality | Offsets require counterfactual, mechanism, lag, interaction and rebound; associative fit alone does not establish savings |

| uncertainty | Parameter, structural, scenario and comparator uncertainty retained; correlated draws and common-cause failures supported |

| validation | Unit, conservation, extreme-case, historical comparator, cross-module reconciliation, face-validity and independent reproduction tests |
11.2.2 Execution order and convergence
Initialize population, comparator policy, capacity/workforce stocks, coverage, fiscal/legal/transition state, formulas and exogenous scenario draws from a versioned manifest.
Generate need/demand; route through coverage, units, specialists, hospitals, products, LTC/BH/DVH/EMS and workforce-constrained capacity; retain unmet demand and queue state.
Adjudicate/payment and financing modules update obligations, outlays, receipts, reserves, burdens and provider liquidity; transition/legal/cyber events may interrupt or redirect flows.
Information/governance modules update data quality, AI state, appeals, safety, trust, formula/legal state, risk indicators and fallback actions; feedback enters the next event/substep.
Outcomes module maps delivered/delayed/omitted care and burdens to outcomes and offsets with explicit lags; reconcile people, services, workforce time, beds/slots, products and money.
Iterate coupled queues, budgets, workforce and financing to declared convergence tolerances or return a nonconvergence finding; never silently force balance by dropping unmet need or obligations.
11.3 State Variables
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: A model cannot reproduce change unless the quantities that persist, accumulate, queue, or transition between periods are explicitly defined. Why this structure: The simulation specification separates model purpose, state, parameters, scenarios, outputs, and input validation so results can be reproduced and contested. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes state variables explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Define the minimum persistent and flow state needed to reproduce system behavior, constraints, transitions and outputs. |

| System entities | MOD-POP through MOD-OUT; authoritative data stewards and model integrator |

| Assumptions | Every shared state has exactly one owning module; other modules consume versioned interfaces. Unmet need, queues, unpaid obligations and failure states are retained. |

| Data / parameters | SV ID/name, definition, owner, unit/type, grain, bounds, initialization, update rule, uncertainty, provenance |

| Requirements / performance | KPP/TPP/CP/RISK/SCN allocations; VR-002–005 |

| Principal risks | hidden state; double ownership; unit mismatch; invalid bounds; suppressed unmet need |

| Simulation implication | Initialize and update typed state arrays; fail validation on unknown IDs, units or incompatible dimensional keys. |
State variables are model memory. Stocks persist across time, flows accumulate over an interval, queue variables retain delay, and output-state variables may be observed at each step. Parameters may influence state transitions but do not become state unless their value evolves endogenously. The 33 source variables below are mandatory; implementations may add extension variables under a namespaced ID.

11.3.1 State-update contract
Each update declares prior state, event/flow inputs, parameter/formula versions, time interval, dimensional keys, stochastic seed/draw, new state and conservation/bound checks.
Stock-flow identities reconcile population, unit/facility/workforce capacity, training pipelines, product inventory, claims/obligations/outlays, receipts/reserves and transition cohorts.
Rates declare numerator, denominator and zero-denominator behavior. Distributions retain percentiles or sufficient statistics; national means cannot overwrite stratified state.
Queues retain arrivals, service capacity, priority/urgency, abandonment, rerouting and completed service. Lost, denied or delayed demand remains observable.
State correction is a versioned event with reason, old/new value, provenance and downstream invalidation/recompute scope; code must not silently coerce invalid values.
11.4 Cost Parameters
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Parameters must carry units, provenance, distributions, correlations, and scenario behavior or different implementations will silently model different systems. Why this structure: The simulation specification separates model purpose, state, parameters, scenarios, outputs, and input validation so results can be reproduced and contested. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes cost parameters explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Bind the complete CP dictionary to modules, units, distributions, time/geographic profiles and accounting reconciliation without inventing values. |

| System entities | MOD-FIN/MOD-OUT and all service/transition modules; HFASB/NHASB/data stewards |

| Assumptions | All 310 source CP records remain controlled. A CP record may be input, calibrated distribution or formula component; computed outputs use OUT IDs and do not overwrite CP definitions. |

| Data / parameters | CP ID/text, family, unit, status, value/distribution, dimensions, time profile, correlation, provenance, formula allocation |

| Requirements / performance | PR-CST-001–010; KPP-C1–C8; VR-024 |

| Principal risks | double counting; false offsets; mixed price bases; transfer/reserve confusion; unbounded correlation |

| Simulation implication | Load CP values through schema records; reconcile family/category totals, accounting views and controlled cost constraints on every run. |
The machine catalog carries all 310 CP records verbatim from the controlled source package. This section organizes them into 20 families and defines how a run supplies values. The framework cost position remains a model constraint: mature total-system cost is approximately $4.75T/year in real 2024 dollars, with a $4.30T–$5.25T plausible range; transition is $1.2T–$2.0T over 10–12 years; first-decade transition-adjusted annual cost is approximately $4.90T–$5.05T/year.

11.4.1 Parameter value contract

| Field | Controlled rule |

| status | One of final_framework_assumption, target, calibrated, external_observation, scenario_assumption, inferred or uncalibrated. |

| value | Provide scalar only when supported; otherwise distribution or explicit uncalibrated status. Unit must agree with CP text/registered override. |

| distribution | Named family or empirical samples; parameters, truncation/bounds, correlation group and seed policy required. |

| dimensions/time | Declare applicable dimensional keys, base period, real/nominal basis, escalation/index and interpolation/extrapolation. |

| provenance | Source reference, version/date, transformation, owner, reviewer, confidence and replacement/supersession relation. |

| formula/allocation | Register equation, sign, category/accounting view, shared-cost rule, transfer elimination and dependent CP/SV/OUT IDs. |
11.4.2 Accounting and offset controls
Total-system, public-budget, operating, capital, transition, household/employer and regional/equity views reconcile but are not interchangeable.
Authority, obligation, outlay, accrual, receipt, internal transfer, reserve contribution/balance/draw and consumed cost remain separate ledger states.
Gross added cost, gross offset and net cost are published separately. Each CP-OFF value needs a counterfactual, causal mechanism, lag, interaction, rebound, displaced cost and capacity/outcome constraint.
Shared labor, facilities, diagnostics, IT, governance and education are allocated once under a registered rule. Cross-module sums fail if duplicated IDs or allocations exceed the shared total.
Every run performs central/range cost checks, category aggregation, public/private consolidation, population/GDP denominator consistency and transition closeout reconciliation.
11.5 Simulation Scenarios
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: The framework should be tested under favorable, central, pessimistic, legal, fiscal, cyber, workforce, and regional conditions rather than one preferred future. Why this structure: The simulation specification separates model purpose, state, parameters, scenarios, outputs, and input validation so results can be reproduced and contested. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes simulation scenarios explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Specify baseline and stress configurations as versioned override sets and event sequences while preserving common denominators and controlled constraints. |

| System entities | Scenario owner; model integrator; NHASB/red team; module owners |

| Assumptions | Scenario codes describe assumptions, not probabilities. Base/optimistic/pessimistic apply broad parameter sets; stress scenarios alter named mechanisms and can be composed only under declared precedence. |

| Data / parameters | SCN ID/version, parent, comparator, horizon, seed, overrides, events, correlations, disabled controls, stop rules, outputs |

| Requirements / performance | SCN catalog; RISK/FMEA; phase/gate rules |

| Principal risks | double injection; inconsistent comparator; impossible combinations; favorable hidden overrides |

| Simulation implication | Compile scenario manifests into parameter/state/event changes; reject conflicting overrides unless explicit precedence and reconciliation are provided. |

11.5.1 Scenario run design
A run identifies comparator (existing_system or NHA), model/schema/code/data versions, horizon, time step, seed stream, scenario and any compound parent/child relation.
Overrides reference CP or SV IDs, dimensions, effective interval, operation (set/add/multiply/draw/event), value/distribution and precedence. An override cannot mutate an output directly.
Common exogenous draws are paired across comparators where appropriate; policy-responsive behavior, capacity and legal/fallback states remain comparator-specific.
Scenario composition checks duplicate targets, incompatible legal/phase states, double-counted demand/capacity shocks, correlated common causes and control/fallback dependencies.
Run ensembles report sampling error, parameter/structural uncertainty and scenario spread separately; scenario results are conditional, not occurrence forecasts.

11.6.1 Output assurance
Return level and comparator difference where meaningful, with central estimate, interval/quantiles, sample count and decomposition of parameter, stochastic and scenario uncertainty.
Attach numerator, denominator, inclusion/exclusion, suppression, weighting and price/time basis. Changing a definition creates a new version and blocks unmarked longitudinal comparison.
Stratify access, safety, appeal, outcome, burden and trust by required vulnerable/protected groups where lawful and ethical; publish suppression/uncertainty rather than collapsing small cells into a national average.
A target or phase-gate result reports pass/fail/indeterminate, margin, evidence completeness, verifier and binding constraint. Indeterminate is not converted to pass.
Cost and fiscal outputs reconcile to CP-TOT/FIN and ledger views; access/outcome outputs reconcile to delivered, delayed, rerouted, abandoned and unmet demand.
11.7 Simulation Input Schema
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Another team or software agent needs a strict input contract so a run can be validated, repeated, compared, and rejected when required evidence is missing. Why this structure: The simulation specification separates model purpose, state, parameters, scenarios, outputs, and input validation so results can be reproduced and contested. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes simulation input schema explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Provide a machine-valid, versioned contract for run metadata, dimensions, modules, state initialization, parameters, scenarios, correlations, provenance and validation. |

| System entities | Model runner; configuration compiler; data pipeline; schema/version registry; validation and independent reproduction teams |

| Assumptions | Draft 2020-12 JSON Schema is the interchange contract. Extensions use namespaced fields or a controlled schema revision; unknown core IDs fail validation. |

| Data / parameters | metadata, dimensions, module_config, initial_state, parameters, scenario, correlations, provenance |

| Requirements / performance | DATA/CP/SV/SCN/MOD identifiers; VR-002/005/025 |

| Principal risks | schema drift; unknown code; unit mismatch; incomplete provenance; invalid override |

| Simulation implication | Validate syntactically, semantically and cross-record before run; persist validated manifest and hash with results. |

| Dimension | Minimum controlled content | Validation rule |

| time | year; phase; quarter/month/event where required | All records carry start/end or period and time basis |

| region | national; state/territory; RHA region; rural/urban/frontier; tribal jurisdiction | Hierarchical IDs; overlapping tribal geography permitted through explicit jurisdiction field |

| population_group | age; risk; income; disability; language; race/ethnicity where lawful/ethical; pregnancy; rurality | Reference group, privacy rule and suppression policy required for comparisons |

| service_category | hospital; unit; specialist; primary; drug; diagnostic; LTC; behavioral; DVH; EMS; public health | Controlled enumeration with extensible version |

| unit_type | A; B; C; D | Required for unit capacity/cost/access records |

| specialty | primary categories plus bottleneck categories | Versioned taxonomy; urgency class separate |

| hospital | facility and service-line categories | Stable facility/service-line IDs; charter/status metadata |

| product | drug; device; diagnostic; supply categories | Product/version, manufacturer/source and therapeutic/substitution group |

| agency | owning ARCH element | Exactly one authoritative owner; verifier may differ |

| scenario | baseline and stress SCN code | Parent/compound scenario and override precedence explicit |
11.7.1 Top-level schema contract

| Object | Required content | Cross-record controls |

| metadata | schema/run/model/data versions, comparator, start/end year, time step, currency basis | end>=start; real-2024 controlled view; version/hash retained |

| dimensions | region, population, services, unit/specialty/hospital/product/agency vocabularies | unique stable IDs; hierarchy/reference and privacy metadata |

| module_config | one record per enabled MOD ID, version, time step and options | module ID known; owned state initialized or generated |

| initial_state | SV ID, dimensional keys, numeric/vector value, unit, period and provenance | owner/unit/bounds/dimensions match state dictionary |

| parameters | CP ID, status, scalar or distribution, unit, dimensions/time and provenance | known CP; exactly one value form unless uncalibrated |

| scenario | SCN ID, seed, overrides and event sequence | override targets CP/SV only; precedence/conflicts resolved |

| correlations | group, member CP/SV IDs and matrix/method | symmetric PSD matrix or registered copula; dimension match |

| provenance | input ID, source type/ref/version/date, transform, owner/reviewer | every supplied value resolves to provenance entry |
VALIDATION LEVELS  Level 1: JSON Schema syntax/types/enums. Level 2: referential integrity, units, dimensions and bounds. Level 3: accounting/conservation and scenario compatibility. Level 4: calibration/evidence and independent reproduction. Only Levels 1–2 are fully executable from this structural package.
11.7.2 Files and use
The machine catalog JSON contains all 33 SVs, all 310 CP source records, 20 scenarios, 29 outputs, 19 modules, dimension definitions and schema-control metadata.
The .schema.json file is a Draft 2020-12 JSON Schema with strict top-level objects, controlled core ID enums and scalar/distribution parameter alternatives.
The example input is validated against the schema and demonstrates a minimal NHA baseline configuration. It is illustrative and not a calibrated policy forecast.
A production implementation must add controlled vocabulary files, unit registry, semantic cross-record validator, signed provenance manifest and schema migration tests.
12. Conclusions
12.1 System Conclusions
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: The architecture's coherence must be judged across institutions and interfaces, not inferred from the existence of many individually specified components. Why this structure: Conclusions are divided by claim domain so an operational finding cannot be misrepresented as fiscal, legal, or empirical proof. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes system conclusions explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | State what the complete architecture establishes, what remains conditional and how success must be assessed across the coupled system. |

| System entities | All ARCH elements; patients/providers/states/tribal nations; NHASB/CHAO/NHAC; model/implementation teams |

| Assumptions | Conceptual completeness does not imply implementation readiness or comparative performance. Conclusions retain status codes and qualifications. |

| Data / parameters | architecture/requirement/interface coverage, KPP/TPP constraints, phase/gate evidence, risk and model readiness |

| Requirements / performance | SN-01–25; PR/SR/VR; ARCH/IF/PH/KPP/TPP |

| Principal risks | fragmentation; premature readiness claims; aggregation; verification capture |

| Simulation implication | Encode conclusions as traceable records; CD/VD conclusions remain hypotheses/conditions in model and dashboards. |
The system conclusion is conditional but substantive: the framework now defines a coherent national public assurance architecture with explicit delivery capacity, financing, rights, transition and repair mechanisms. Its central design choice is to treat coverage, capacity, payment, information, legitimacy and adaptation as coupled. The same choice creates a demanding verification burden—success cannot be inferred from enrollment, spending or a single national average.
Table D8A-04. System conclusions

| ID | Conclusion | Status | Basis / trace | Decision implication | Principal qualification |

| 62-C01 | The framework is a coupled public assurance and delivery system, not only a payer substitution. | AD | ARCH-DNHA/THDO/NCDTN/NSAA/NHSA/PCU; Sections 4–6 | Treat coverage, payment, capacity, information, governance and transition as one architecture. | Fragmented implementation can preserve current failure modes under a public payer. |

| 62-C02 | Public default coverage and zero or near-zero point-of-care cost are conditional on prior capacity and continuity readiness. | FA/TG | ASM-003/006/007; Gates 1–3/7–8 | Sequence financial-access reform with staffed service capacity and rights readiness. | Premature demand release can create queues, unsafe diversion or hidden rationing. |

12.1.1 System-level determination
Architecture adequacy: sufficient for integrated long-form specification, traceability and simulation implementation planning.
Operational adequacy: indeterminate until regional capacity, workforce, data, payment and continuity evidence pass applicable gates.
Comparative effectiveness: indeterminate until existing-system comparator data and the executable NHA model are calibrated and validated.
Implementation authority: incomplete until bill text, conforming changes, appropriations/revenue provisions and intergovernmental/tribal instruments are enacted or otherwise lawfully established.
Decision use: appropriate for design review, requirements allocation, research planning and simulation construction; not yet appropriate for claiming realized national outcomes.
12.2 Fiscal Conclusions
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Fiscal feasibility depends on scope, transition treatment, revenue, reserves, and uncertainty; no single central cost figure establishes sustainability. Why this structure: Conclusions are divided by claim domain so an operational finding cannot be misrepresented as fiscal, legal, or empirical proof. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes fiscal conclusions explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.

The fiscal architecture is specified well enough to model, but not yet to certify. The framework fixes the cost boundary and controlled central/range assumptions, identifies 310 parameters, separates economic cost from public cash and reserve stocks, and defines a layered financing design. It intentionally leaves numeric category allocation, revenue bases/rates/yields, behavioral response and several reserve formulas open for calibration and legislation.

12.2.1 Fiscal determination
CURRENT FISCAL FINDING  The framework establishes a coherent, testable fiscal hypothesis—not a completed federal score. A mature central total-system cost of approximately $4.75T/year remains the controlled design assumption. Sufficiency, incidence and sustainability are verification-dependent.
A valid score must reconcile mature, first-decade, transition, capital, public-outlay, receipt, transfer and reserve views without double counting.
It must test central and adverse cost, collection, legal, macroeconomic, workforce and demand scenarios and preserve ordinary-household and service-continuity constraints.
It must publish gross additions, offsets, uncertainty and denominator choices and permit independent reproduction by NHASB/CHAO or equivalent external scorekeepers.
12.3 Operational Conclusions
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Operational success requires real capacity, payment continuity, supply, workforce, data, and remedy performance—not enactment or enrollment alone. Why this structure: Conclusions are divided by claim domain so an operational finding cannot be misrepresented as fiscal, legal, or empirical proof. Operationally, the framework is a staged national service transformation. Enrollment and benefit expansion depend on claims and payment rails, staffed diagnostic-treatment units, specialist routing, hospital readiness, product continuity, workforce and rights. Phase gates formalize that dependency and make delay or rollback a designed safety action rather than an implementation failure.

12.3.1 Operational maturity test
Capacity is service-ready only when facilities, people, equipment, supplies, systems, referral/transport interfaces and continuity fallbacks all operate within controlled service levels.
A fallback is operational only when authority, funding, staffing, data, contracts, communications, reconciliation and RTO have been demonstrated.
A national pass requires regional/population distributions and cannot offset a failed protected-group, rural, tribal, active-treatment, safety or payment-continuity constraint with favorable performance elsewhere.
Maturity monitoring continues after P8 and reopens corrective action or gate review when formulas, demand, workforce, technology, law or trust materially change.
12.4 Legal Conclusions
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Legal text is effective only if authorities, duties, standing, remedies, funding protections, and fallbacks survive implementation and challenge. Why this structure: Conclusions are divided by claim domain so an operational finding cannot be misrepresented as fiscal, legal, or empirical proof. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes legal conclusions explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.

The legal conclusion is architectural, not doctrinal: achieving the framework requires a comprehensive statute, extensive conforming amendments, enforceable rights and mandatory fiscal/operational duties. Durability is created through layered defaults and remedies, while adaptability is preserved through transparent, bounded repair. The exact validity and wording of those mechanisms require legislative counsel and specialized constitutional, tax, appropriations, federalism, tribal and administrative-law analysis.

12.4.1 Legal readiness determination
Architecture readiness: sufficient to allocate legislative subjects, authorities, duties, remedies, migration and fallback dependencies.
Drafting readiness: partial; definitions, operative clauses, jurisdiction, appropriations classifications, tax bases, preemption standards, severability and conforming citations remain open.
Litigation resilience: indeterminate until primary and fallback authorities are reviewed and exercised with operational owners and quantified replacement effects.
Tribal readiness: dependent on nation-to-nation consultation, consent mechanisms, direct funding/data governance and tribal-approved compact evidence.

The workforce conclusion is unequivocal at the architectural level: labor capacity is one of the framework's principal binding constraints. Facilities, benefits, funding and technology cannot deliver care without role-specific people in the right regions and settings. The framework therefore couples education expansion, compensation, safe workload, scope reform, transition protection and regional planning—but numeric adequacy remains calibration-dependent.

12.5.2 Workforce maturity determination
The <=5% critical-vacancy target must be met with safe workload and service performance by region, occupation and setting; an aggregate national result is insufficient.
Pipeline adequacy includes faculty, placement capacity, completion, licensure, geographic/service uptake, attrition and time to independent practice—not training-slot announcements alone.
Transition protection includes displaced administrative workers and workers whose roles, employers, payment systems or scope change; placement and retention outcomes remain auditable.
Workforce savings are valid only when labor time is genuinely released or redeployed without shifting unpaid work to clinicians, caregivers, patients or communities.

WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: The specification establishes what may be tested, but it cannot honestly claim comparative results until code, data, calibration, validation, and uncertainty runs exist. Why this structure: Conclusions are divided by claim domain so an operational finding cannot be misrepresented as fiscal, legal, or empirical proof. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes simulation conclusions explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.

The simulation conclusion is procedural rather than numerical. The framework now contains enough structure for another AI or software team to implement a comparative model. It does not yet contain a calibrated executable model, so it cannot establish comparative cost, access, safety or equity outcomes. Its strongest current contribution is a controlled contract for building and auditing such a model.

| 67-C05 | Access, safety, rights, workforce, tribal, fiscal and continuity constraints must bind cost optimization and scenario interpretation. | DUTY | KPP/TPP; Gates 1–8; No Silent Rationing; VR-025 | Reject solutions that lower cost by unmet need, unsafe staffing, unpaid obligations or prohibited burden. | Unconstrained optimization can reward harm. |

| 67-C06 | Unmet demand, queues, abandoned care, delayed payment, reserve draws, legal constraints and fallback use are state variables or events, not missing data. | DUTY | SV/OUT dictionaries; RISK/FMEA; legal-state model | Persist and report these states with regional/population distribution. | Dropping them creates false savings and resilience. |

| 67-C07 | Scenarios are conditional tests rather than assigned forecasts or occurrence probabilities. | PROTECTION | SCN-BASE/OPT/PESS and 17 stress scenarios; SCN-RT-01–10 | Report scenario assumptions, override magnitudes and uncertainty separately from probability. | Users may read a pessimistic/optimistic case as a confidence interval. |

| 67-C08 | Model validation must be layered: schema, referential/unit, accounting/conservation, calibration, historical/comparator fit and independent reproduction. | EVIDENCE | D7C validation levels; VR-002–005 | Publish failed/indeterminate checks and model-use limits with each release. | Schema validity alone says nothing about causal or predictive validity. |

| 67-C09 | Risk controls and legal/operational fallbacks receive credit only when their dependencies and activation/recovery performance are represented or exercised. | EVIDENCE | RISK/FMEA; LF-01–11; SCN-RT | Model authority, people, assets, data, funding, activation lag, RTO and residual effects. | Named fallbacks can overstate resilience. |

| 67-C10 | The model is decision support for design, stress testing and research prioritization; it is not an individual clinical tool, legal opinion or automatic budget score. | PROTECTION | OBJ-06; D7C non-use rule | Enforce governance, versioning, audit, reproducibility and prohibited-use controls. | Results can be overextended beyond model scope. |
12.6.1 Permitted future conclusion upgrades
Structural result: may be reported after schema, unit, referential and conservation validation.
Calibrated baseline result: additionally requires authoritative data, parameter estimation, uncertainty and historical/comparator fit.
Comparative result: additionally requires aligned comparators, paired scenarios, sensitivity/structural alternatives and independent reproduction.
Policy-readiness result: additionally requires legal/fiscal review, phase/gate evidence, stakeholder testing and explicit non-use/decision thresholds.
Observed implementation result: requires actual operational data and must not be inferred from preimplementation simulation alone.
13. Implications
13.1 Implications for Patients
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Patients experience the system as appointments, bills, records, explanations, and remedies; institutional design must be translated into those everyday changes. Why this structure: Implications are organized by affected group so aggregate national gains do not conceal local burdens, duties, or transition risks. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes implications for patients explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.
Section control record

| Control field | Controlled content |

| Purpose | Translate the framework into patient-facing coverage, access, continuity, affordability, rights, data and transition consequences with measurable safeguards. |

| System entities | Covered persons; caregivers; DNHA/RHA; units/providers/hospitals/pharmacies; NOPRSL/ombudsmen/courts |

| Assumptions | Covered status alone is insufficient; implications require usable delivered care and accessible remedies, stratified for vulnerable populations. |

| Data / parameters | eligibility, billing/debt, access/wait, transfer, medication, explanation/appeal, records/AI, safety/equity/trust |

| Requirements / performance | SN-01–05/08/14–20; KPP/TPP; Patient Bill of Rights |

| Principal risks | queueing; benefit ambiguity; transition loss; privacy/AI harm; inaccessible remedies |

| Simulation implication | Report OUT-009–029 and patient journeys by region/population under base/stress scenarios. |
For patients, the framework aims to replace financial and insurance fragmentation with continuous public assurance and a more organized path to care. The trade is not merely financial: patients interact with public enrollment, unit networks, referral rules, national formularies, a shared information mesh and public appeals. Those institutions must be understandable, accessible and accountable for the promised protection to be real.
Table D8B-05. Patient implications

| ID | Controlled implication | Type | Basis / trace | Verification measure | Qualification / risk |

| 68-I01 | Core coverage becomes a public default that is not tied to employment, income churn or insurer status. | OUTCOME/CHANGE | SN-02; ASM-003; KPP-A1 | continuous core coverage >=99.5% | Eligibility/data error or exclusion can still disrupt practical access. |

| 68-I02 | Covered medically necessary care carries zero or near-zero point-of-care cost, with covered-care billing and debt tightly constrained. | OUTCOME/PROTECTION | SN-01; ASM-006; KPP-A3/A4 | billing <=0.5% of covered encounters; new covered-care debt <=1% | Coverage boundaries, miscoding and legacy debt require appeal/restitution. |

| 68-I03 | Common care should be available through Type A–D units with same-day pathways, diagnostics, follow-up and escalation. | OUTCOME | SN-03; NCDTN; KPP-B2 | same-day low-acuity access >=85%; follow-up closure | Underbuilt/staff-poor units can convert financial access into queues. |

| 68-I04 | Specialist access is routed through structured packets, urgency classes, e-consults, tele-specialty and protected urgent slots. | CHANGE/OUTCOME | SN-04; NSAA; KPP-B5/B6 | routine median <=30 days; urgent timeliness >=95% | Routing may under-refer or shift work unless audited for safety/equity. |

| 68-I05 | Active treatment, medications, referrals and care plans receive continuity protection during payer and system conversion. | TRANSITION/PROTECTION | SN-05; Patient Continuity Guarantee; KPP-T1 | active-treatment transfer success >=99% | Record/authorization failure may still require provisional coverage and manual repair. |

| 68-I06 | Essential medications receive real-time public claims and no-interruption transition rules, with reviewed substitution where necessary. | OUTCOME/PROTECTION | SN-08; PCU; pharmacy continuity rule | medication access and shortage exposure; emergency-fill success | Shortages, formulary change and pharmacy outages remain material risks. |

| 68-I07 | Denial, delay, rerouting and non-referral decisions must be visible, explained, appealable and audited. | DUTY/PROTECTION | SN-14; No Silent Rationing; TPP-LEG1 | explanation completeness >=98%; appeal usability/timeliness | Formal rights may fail if services are inaccessible or appeal relief is too slow. |

| 68-I08 | Patients receive record access, correction, segmentation, sensitive-use audit and human review of high-stakes AI-supported decisions. | PROTECTION | SN-15/17; Health Data Rights Charter; ASM-009 | correction closure >=97%; sensitive audit/high-stakes review >=99% | Privacy, identity mismatch, cyber incidents and automation bias require active remedies. |

| 68-I09 | Benefits expand across LTC, behavioral health/SUD, dental, vision, hearing, EMS and clinically linked supports. | OUTCOME | SN-03/18/19; expanded service concepts | domain-specific timely delivered care and equity metrics | Nominal coverage may exceed workforce and regional capacity. |

| 68-I10 | Patient success is measured by delivered safe care, continuity, affordability, rights and equity—not enrollment alone. | EVIDENCE | KPP/TPP; OUT-009–029; VR-004/010/012 | stratified access/safety/outcome/trust and patient-burden evidence | National averages can conceal disability, language, rural, tribal or income barriers. |
PATIENT CONTROL  No patient benefit is counted as realized when care is nominally covered but unavailable, delayed beyond the clinical standard, financially misbilled, inaccessible because of disability/language/digital barriers, or unsupported by usable explanation and appeal.
13.2 Implications for Providers
WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS  Why it is needed: Providers need to understand how payment, workload, documentation, referral, autonomy, review, and transition protections change—not merely that coverage expands. Why this structure: Implications are organized by affected group so aggregate national gains do not conceal local burdens, duties, or transition risks. Improvement mechanism: compared with the current fragmented arrangement, this section makes implications for providers explicit, allocates responsibility, and exposes the claim to requirements, verification, risk analysis, and simulation rather than leaving it as an aspiration.

| Purpose | Translate changes to payment, administration, clinical accountability, routing, compensation, information, remedies and transition obligations. |

| System entities | Clinicians and teams; provider organizations; NCCA/THDO; NCDTN/NSAA; workforce bodies; NHAC/A1-HCAC |

| Assumptions | Administrative simplification and predictable payment are targets, not assumed outcomes; transition dual-run and public accountability may add work before savings are realized. |
